en: Now begins the first chapter of the first book.
Regarding this, it has been said: "The Huta, the Prahuta, the Āhuta, the Śūlagava, the Bali-haraṇa, the Pratyavarohaṇa, and the Aṣṭakā-homa—these are the seven forms of the Pākayajña.
We shall explain these in detail. 1–2.
In that regard, that which is offered by pouring is the *huta*, such as this [rite of] marriage and the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*).

For in those cases, it is indeed offered by pouring. (3–4) Now, that which is given after having been offered is the *prahuta*, such as this [rite of] birth-observance (*jātakarman*) and the tonsure (*caula*). (5)
For in that case, it is indeed given after having been offered. 6.
Now, that which is both offered and given and then taken is called *āhuta*, such as this initiation (*upanayana*) and the return home (*samāvartana*). 7.
For in those cases, it is both offered and given and then taken. 8.
Now, when they bring [the animal] to the stakes and cook the products of the cow, that is the *śūlagava* (stake-animal sacrifice). 9.

Now, when they scatter food for the domestic deities, that is the *baliharaṇa* (offering of oblations). 10. Now, when they descend from season to season, that is the *pratyavarohaṇa* (rite of descending). 11.

Now, that food which is prepared on the Ekāṣṭakā day is called the Aṣṭakā-homa. 12. We shall now explain the marriage ceremony. 13. During the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, he sends out even-numbered Brahmins as suitors with the verse: "May the prayers of him who offers [the sacrifice] be successful; may you, O suitors, approach the excellent bridegrooms. May Indra enjoy both our offerings when he takes notice of the Soma-juice. 14.
Since he recites the mantra: "May the paths be thornless and straight by which our friends go to choose a bride; may Aryaman and Saṃbhaga lead us [to her]; O Gods, may our household be well-governed.
(15) Now, if she has been given along with wedding gifts (*dakṣiṇā*), one should not send for suitors here.
(16) He should receive her with these six verses according to their meters, beginning with: "Prajāpati is the glory in women... (17)
All months are suitable for marriage. 18. According to some, this excludes the months of Śuci, Tapas, and Tapasya. 19.
Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, the two Uttarā-phalgunīs, and Svātī are the lunar mansions for marriage. 20.
Punarvasū, Tiṣya, Hasta, Śroṇā, and Revatī are for other rites intended for prosperity (bhūtikarma). 21.

On whichever other auspicious constellations are prescribed, one should feed an even number of Brāhmaṇas on the day before those rites of prosperity and merit (vṛddhi-pūrta). 22. The service [of the guests] should be performed in a clockwise direction. 23.

Having strewn the ground with barley mixed with flowers, fruits, and unbroken grains for the sake of the sesame offering, having scattered curd-rice, having placed his right knee on the ground and raised his left, having murmured the mantra "Iḍā devahūḥ," and having caused [the Brahmins] to recite, "May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be pleased," he should serve food to the Brahmins, saying, "Today is the wedding. Then, having caused them to recite three times each the blessings preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*—"An auspicious day! Welfare! Prosperity!"—he, bathed, wearing new clothes, anointed with perfume, and adorned with a garland, [proceeds].

Having eaten, with the goad in hand and on foot, he goes and is honored like a guest by the bride’s kinsmen. He gazes upon the bride who has been bathed, dressed in unwashed garments, anointed with perfumes, adorned with garlands, and having eaten; she is handed over with arrows in her hand, [with the mantra]: "O Bṛhaspati, O Varuṇa, O Indra, O Savitṛ, grant her to this man as one who does not kill her brother, nor her husband, nor her sons, and who is Lakṣmī herself. (24) While being gazed upon by her, he mutters: "Be thou of non-terrible eye, not a slayer of thy husband, auspicious toward thy husbands, well-disposed, full of luster, a mother of living sons, desiring the gods, pleasant; be a source of welfare to our bipeds and welfare to our quadrupeds. (25)

Then, with a blade of *darbha* grass, he wipes her between the eyebrows and the mouth, saying: "O woman, whatever ill fortune (*alakṣmī*) there is in you that makes you a slayer of your husband, that I now point out.
(26) Having cast away the *darbha* grass and touched water, he then takes her by the right hand, saying: "Thou art Mitra. (27)

Then he leads her to the place of sacrifice (devayajana), saying: "One step for sap—may Viṣṇu follow you; two steps for strength—may Viṣṇu follow you; three steps for the vow—may Viṣṇu follow you; four steps for well-being—may Viṣṇu follow you; five steps for cattle—may Viṣṇu follow you; six steps for the nourishment of food—may Viṣṇu follow you; seven steps for the seven priestly offices—may Viṣṇu follow you.

Having grasped the seventh step, he murmurs: "We have become companions through seven steps; may I attain your friendship; may I not be separated from your friendship; may you not be separated from my friendship."
Thus ends the first chapter of the first book in the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the second chapter of the first book:
Having announced [the guest], one should offer the arghya water. 1.

In the middle of the house, he spreads out *erakā* grass facing north. (2) Having spread upon them unwashed garments that are many-threaded and have their fringes turned toward the north, the officiating priests sit upon them facing east.
(3) In the northeastern part of the house, having strewn *darbha* grass with its points directed eastward, he arranges the materials for the *arghya* offering upon them. (4)

There should be as many bronze vessels with lids as there are officiating priests, and as many bundles of grass (kūrca). 5. There should be two additional bundles of grass for the purpose of receiving [the water]. 6. [The materials required are:
curd, honey, clarified butter, water, milk, pairs of garments, and pairs of earrings. 7.
The milk of such a cow [is used] for the cup, the garland, and the ornament.

(8) Having prepared the strainers, having silently purified the vessels with consecrated water, having turned them face upwards and sprinkled them, and having placed the bronze vessel upon a grass mat, he pours honey through the strainers.
(9) Curd or milk is the second [substance]; that is the "twofold" (dvivṛt). (10)
Clarified butter is the third; he is the threefold (trivṛt). What is the second [the day] is the fourth; he is the fourfold (caturvṛt).
Water is the fifth; he is the fivefold (pāṅkta).
Having covered [the student] with a large, radiant [blanket], various men, following behind him as he walks along, take up the materials for the *arghya* offering. 14.
"A grass mat (*kūrca*)," he says, referring to the mat. 15.
"A good grass mat (*sukūrca*)," the other replies, as he receives it. 16.
Having circumambulated it clockwise and turned toward the north, he sits down.
Or rather, from the east, he pushes the stool westward with the formula: "Thou art the Rāṣṭrabhṛt; thou art the teacher’s stool; may I not injure thee.
Then, having taken a water-pot for him and grasped it with two grass-blades (kūrca), he announces: "The waters for washing the feet."
He consecrates them with the mantra: "O waters, wash my feet; may you destroy my enemy. May I be endowed with spiritual luster in this family.
(20) He extends his right foot first to a Brāhmaṇa; to a Śūdra, he extends it himself.
(21) A woman washes [the feet], and a man sprinkles [water over them]; according to some, it is the reverse. (22)
23. By rule, the wife and the sacrificer cause their shins to be washed.

24. He touches the hands of the one who has washed them with the formula: "In me be greatness; in me be fortune; in me be splendor; in me be glory. 25. Then, having touched water, he touches himself toward his chest with the formula: "In me be power and vigor."
Having mixed water with rice or barley grains, and having grasped it with two blades of grass as before, he says, "The waters worthy of honor.
(26) He consecrates them with the mantra: "It has come, O Āmā, with luster and glory; unite me with milk and splendor. Make me dear to all creatures, the lord of cattle.
(27) He consecrates a portion being poured into his joined palms with the mantra: "Thou art Virāj; may I obtain the milking of Virāj; for my footstep, [may there be] Virāj. (28)

I consecrate with a mantra the remaining waters being carried away toward the west: "I send you forth to the ocean; go to your own source, O imperishable ones! May I be unbroken in my progeny; may your water not fail me.

(29) Then, having likewise grasped them with two *kūrca* grass-bunches, he announces: "These are the waters for the under-layer. (30) He drinks them with: "Thou art the under-layer of immortality. (31)

He should sip water three times and wipe [his mouth] three times; some say twice. (32) To him who has sipped water and turned away, [the host], having likewise taken hold of two grass-blades (*kūrca*), says: "The *arghya*," or "The *madhuparka*. (33) He recites the consecration formula over the announced *madhuparka*: "Thou art the glory of the triple knowledge (*trayī vidyā*); thou art the glory of glory; thou art the radiance of Brahman. Make me dear to all creatures, and the lord of cattle. (34)
He receives it with both hands, saying: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I receive thee.

(35) If anything should fall upon it, he grasps it with his thumb and his ring finger and casts it away toward this direction (the south), saying: "O Neṣṭṛ, I cut off thy prosperity; with that form of thine which is terrible, enter him who hates us and whom we hate. (36)

Then, having touched water and having mixed it with all his fingers, he eats it, [thinking]: "Whatever sweetness of honey, supreme food-strength, and vigor there is—by that sweetness of honey, by that supreme food-strength and vigor, may I become the most excellent eater of food, full of sweetness. (37) Having eaten it three times, he should drink the remainder three times.
(38) He should give the remainder to one who desires what is better for himself. (39)
When he has sipped water and turned away, [the teacher] likewise takes hold of the two blades of grass and says, "The waters are for covering.
40. He drinks them with the formula, "Thou art the immortal covering. 41. He should sip water three times and wipe his mouth three times; some say twice. 42.
When he has sipped water and turned away, [the teacher] says "Cow" regarding the cow.
43. He consecrates her with the mantra: "Thou art a cow; thou art one whose evil has been struck down; drive away the evil of both myself and so-and-so," and he utters the name of the student.
44. He announces the cows separately to each of the major officiating priests. 45.
One [portion] for the Hotṛs.
Or rather, one [portion] for all, because of the lack of sufficient resources.

He who has spoken [the invocation], for him he performs the dedication (*upākaraṇa*). He offers a portion of the omentum (*vapā*) with the verse: "May Agni eat first; for he knows how the oblation is. May he, who is observed by all, make the plants auspicious for us. (TS 3.1.4.4)

He offers a portion and eats it [with the mantra]: "May Agni eat first; for he knows how the oblation is. May he make us free from harm—this Brāhmaṇa among Brāhmaṇas. Then, when he is about to release her, he addresses her with the mantra: "The cow is to be a milch-cow; she is the mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Ādityas, and the navel of immortality. I have declared this to the wise person: do not slay the cow, the sinless Aditi. Let her drink water and eat grass. Om! Release her! When she has been released, he sacrifices a ram or a goat.
Or with forest meat. (52) But one should never be without meat. (53) In case of inability, flour-based food may be prepared. (54)
When [the guest] has said, "It is prepared," [the host] says, "It is well-prepared.
(56) He consecrates that [food] with the mantra: "It is prepared, it is well-prepared; she is Virāj. May it not fail me; may I enjoy it; may it provide me with strength and vigor—Oṃ, prepare it! (57)
He should say, "Feed four Brahmins of various lineages.
58. When they have eaten, he offers food to him.
59. He consumes it with the formula: "Thou art Virāj; food is Virāj; as Virāj, bestow the splendor of Virāj upon me. 60.

To those who have eaten, he should give pairs of garments and pairs of earrings, as well as a cow whose milk is in a cup, a garland, and ornaments. Some say he should give a "single-wealth" cow that has six calves, or two young bulls. (61) Some authorities prescribe the giving of ornaments before the *madhuparka* offering. (62) One should honor the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and the teacher (*ācārya*), or one honors oneself by honoring the officiating priest and the teacher; such indeed are the lifelong vows, or they may be temporary. The causes for exclusion are: one who has fallen from his caste (*patita*) and one who has not studied the Veda (*ananūcāna*). (63)
In the *varaṇa* ceremony and in rites beginning with the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), one should remember these as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

Likewise, these are worthy of the guest-offering (*arghya*): the officiating priest, the father-in-law, the paternal uncle, the maternal uncle, the teacher, the king, the accomplished student (*snātaka*), a beloved suitor, and a guest.
One should act in this manner toward these very persons when they arrive after a year has passed, and toward the suitor at a wedding.
Then he gives gifts to the officiating priests after each ritual act.
Thus ends the second chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the third chapter in the first book.
Then, on a pure and level spot, he should mark out the site for the fire-altar with a wooden splinter, scratching it three times toward the east and three times toward the north.

(1) Then, having sprinkled it with water and cast away the splinter, and having touched water, he should produce fire by friction from a sacrificial log or fetch it from the house of a learned Vedic scholar; having established it with the *vyāhṛtis* and added fuel, he stands over it [reciting]:
(2) "May the beloved, domestic guest, dwelling in the home, come to this our sacrifice, being wise. O Agni, having struck down all assailants, bring hither the food of those who act as enemies. (3)
Then, having swept around the fire from left to right, having wiped it around, and having strewn grass around it, he strews darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward around the fire.

(4) Or else, the tips point northward; those at the back and those at the front are so. (5) If the tips point both east and north, then the southern blades are placed above and the northern ones below. (6)

To the north of the fire, having strewn darbha grass with the tips pointing eastward, he places the vessels upon them in pairs, turned face down: those connected with the gods one by one, those connected with the ancestors likewise, and those connected with humans all at once. (7) This is based on the Brāhmaṇa passage: "Because all human [vessels] are together.

(8) Having prepared two strainers and silently purified the vessels with consecrated water, having turned the vessels face up and sprinkled them, he unties the fuel-bundle and sprinkles it three times with all the water. (9)

A Brāhmaṇa sits on *darbha* grass to the south, and a vessel of water to the north. (10) Then, having poured the clarified butter into the butter-pot across the strainers, having drawn out embers toward the north, having made them into a pit, having placed [the pot] over them, having illuminated it with a lighting-stick, having cut off two tips of *darbha* grass, having washed them and thrown them back [into the fire], having illuminated it again, having carried fire around it three times while making a path, having removed it toward the north, and having pushed back the embers, he spreads the sacrificial grass. Then, having purified it three times by moving it back and forth with two strainers whose tips point northward, he unties the strainers.
Having touched it with water, he throws it into the fire.

(11) Then, having heated the ladle, wiped it with *darbha* grass, touched it with water, heated it again, sprinkled it, and set it down, he touches the *darbha* blades with water and throws them into the fire.

(12) Then he places the *śamyā* pegs as enclosing sticks: one made of *khadira* wood for one who desires splendor, one of *udumbara* wood for one who desires food, and one of *pālāśa* wood for one who desires spiritual luster. (13)

Now, regarding this, some have the following tradition: "The ladle (*darvī*) is indeed seized by Nirṛti; if one were to offer with a ladle, he would cause the sacrifice to be seized by Nirṛti. Therefore, one should offer only with a dipping-spoon (*sruva*).
(14) "With a *sruva* made of *pālāśa* wood," says Ātreya. (15) "With one made of *khādira* wood," says Āṅgirasa. (16)
"With copper and iron," says the Atharvavedin (17). "With black iron when practicing sorcery," is the universal rule (18).
Or another [may do so], having performed this much, should desire his arrival (19).

To the west [of the fire], having spread out an Erakā-grass mat with its fringes directed toward the north and perfumed with incense, they both sit upon it facing east—the husband to the north and the wife to the south.
Then, while she maintains contact with him, he sprinkles water around the fire from left to right:
"O Aditi, give your consent," thus on the south side, pouring eastward.

With the words, "O Anumati, give your consent," he [draws the line] behind, directed toward the north. With the words, "O Sarasvatī, give your consent," he draws it from the north, directed toward the east.
With the words, "O God Savitṛ, impel," he draws it all around in a clockwise direction, or indeed all around silently.

Having anointed the two [pieces of wood] for the gods, he leaves one as the *parisamidh* (the enclosing fuel-stick). Having added them with the utterance of *svāhā*, he pours the two *āghāra* libations.
(26) With the formula "To Prajāpati, svāhā," he touches [the fire] obliquely and continuously at the northern junction of the enclosing sticks, mentally.
(27) With the formula "To Indra, svāhā," pronounced in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), he touches [the fire] obliquely and continuously at the southern junction of the enclosing sticks. (28)
Then he offers the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga):
29. With "To Agni, svāhā! on the eastern part of the northern half; 30. With "To Soma, svāhā! on the eastern part of the southern half. 31.

Then he offers into the mouth of the fire (agnimukha). 32. "Yoked, O Jātavedas, carry [the oblation] forward; O Agni, know this rite as it is being performed. You are the physician, the maker of the remedy; through you, may we obtain cattle, horses, and men for all time. Svāhā! 33. "Let the four quarters proceed; let Agni, knowing [the way], lead this sacrifice of ours. Drinking the clarified butter, undecaying, and rich in heroes—may the sacred word (*brahman*) become the fuel for the oblations. Svāhā! 34.

May auspicious intentions come to us from every side—intentions that are undeceivable, unassailable, and victorious. O gods, just as you have always been present for our prosperity, may you be our protectors day by day, extending our lives. Svāhā! 35 O Virūpākṣa, do not cause us distress; do not oppress us, for you have already oppressed us. They say you are the son of Nirṛti; hold fast our vital organs for us. Svāhā! 36 I worship Virūpākṣa, whose legs are bent and whose belly is variegated—he who constantly oppresses me. To him, for the sake of fortune and nourishment, Svāhā! 37
"You who lie across, saying 'I am the destroyer'—you, I worship with a stream of clarified butter in the fire, O *saṃrādhinī*, Svāhā!

(38) "To the goddess *Saṃrādhinī*, Svāhā! To the goddess *Prasādhinī*, Svāhā! Bhūḥ Svāhā! Bhuvaḥ Svāhā! Suvaḥ Svāhā! Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ Svāhā! This much is the ritual procedure for all *darvī-homa* offerings. (39) Thus ends the third chapter of the first book in the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhya Sūtra.
Now begins the fourth chapter of the first book.

Then, having approached her, he places his right hand upon her right shoulder, drawing it down along her arm, and touches the region of her heart with the mantra: "May your heart be in my heart; may your mind be in my mind. Listen to me with a single-minded focus; devoted to me alone, be my companion.
(1) Then he mutters [the following] into her right ear. (2)
May your mind enter into me; may your eye [enter] me; may your fortune enter me. May all beings be in me; may your wisdom be in me.
(3) O honey-sweet one, O you who plunge into honey, may my tongue be a speaker of honey. May the honey of the bees be in my mouth; the charm for winning over has been performed upon those who eat.
(4) The charm for winning over that belongs to the ruddy geese and which is drawn from the rivers—by that which the gods and Gandharvas know, may we two be united in love. (5)
I touch your limbs; may the wind and the waters protect you from death. Behold me and the sun, and do not set your heart on others.
(6) Soma first obtained her; Gandharva obtained her next. Agni was your third husband; your fourth is born of man.
(7) Soma gave her to Gandharva; Gandharva gave her to Agni. And Agni has given her to me, along with wealth and sons. (8)
“O Sarasvatī, protect this [sacrifice], O blessed one, rich in prizes! As such, we sing forth to you at the head of all that exists.

(9) Then, with his right hand lowered, he takes her right hand—turned upward—with its thumb, as if over the hair, saying: “I take your hand for the sake of good offspring, so that you may reach old age with me as your husband. Bhaga, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Purandhi—the gods have given you to me for the household. (10)

Then he leads her clockwise around the fire with the verse: "O Agni, we set thee around us as a fortress, thee the sage, O powerful one; thee of bold color, day by day, the breaker of the treacherous.
(11) Then, having sat down in that manner while she holds on to him, he offers the *upayamani* oblations while she maintains contact:
(12) "O Agni, be strong for great good fortune; may thy splendors be most excellent. Make our household lordship well-governed; trample down the powers of those who act as enemies. *Svāhā*! (13)
To Soma, the knower of birth, svāhā! 14.
To the Gandharva, the knower of birth, svāhā! 15. To Agni, the knower of birth, svāhā! 16.
When the maiden went from her parents to the world of her husband, you bestowed upon her consecration; Svāhā!
17 May he release her from there, having loosened her well-bound [cord] from that place. So that she, being blessed with good sons and fortunate, may praise Indra;
Svāhā! 18 O bountiful Indra, make this woman possessed of good sons and fortune. Bestow ten sons upon her, and let the husband be the eleventh; Svāhā! 19

May Agni come first among the deities; may he release her offspring from the noose of death. Thus may this woman not weep over the misfortune of losing a son. Svāhā! (20) May Agni Gārhapatya protect her; may he lead her offspring to a long life. May she have a living mother with an unfailing lap; may she awaken to the joy of seeing her grandson. Svāhā! (21)

"Let no cry arise in your house at night; let those who weep settle elsewhere than with you. Do not wail with disheveled hair upon your breast; as one whose husband is living, shine forth in the world of your husband, beholding your offspring with a well-disposed mind. Svāhā! (22) Childlessness, the death of a grandson, evil, or even sin—I cast this away like a garland from my head and fasten the bond upon my enemies. Svāhā! (23)

Then, having raised her up, he makes her step upon a stone with her right foot to the north of the fire, [saying]: "Step upon this stone; like a stone, may you be firm. Overcome those who attack you; subdue those who seek battle.
(24) Then, having spread a layer [of ghee] in her joined palms, her uterine brother pours fried grains (*lāja*) into them twice.

(25) Having sprinkled them [with ghee], he offers them [into the fire, saying]: "This woman speaks here, pouring fried grains into the fire: 'May my husband have a long life; may he live for a hundred autumns, Svāhā! (26)

Then he leads her around the fire clockwise with the verse: "O Agni, they have led the bride around for you, together with the bridal procession; O Agni, give her back to her husbands along with offspring. (27) He establishes her in that manner and offers the oblation in that manner.

(28) Then he leads her again around the fire clockwise with the verse: "Agni has given the wife back again, together with long life and splendor; may the husband of this woman attain a hundred autumns of long life. (29)
He establishes it in that very same way and offers the oblation in that very same way.
(30) Then he again causes her to mount [the chariot] with the verse: "May we, through you, overcome all enemies, as flowing streams overcome water.
(31) Then, having sat down in that manner while she holds on to him from behind, and having offered the *jayas*, *abhyātānas*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛts*, he then offers the *āmātya* oblations. (32)
Then he offers the oblation to Prajāpati with the verse: "O Prajāpati, none other than you... (RV 10.121.10).

Then he offers the Sviṣṭakṛt oblation with the verse: "Whatever in this rite I have done in excess, or whatever I have done here deficiently—may Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the wise one, make all that well-sacrificed and well-offered for me. To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the consumer of well-offered oblations, the fulfiller of the desires of the offerings, svāhā!
Then he anoints the enclosing sticks with the sruva-ladle.

Then, having smeared around the place of the strewn grass and having cut a blade of sacrificial grass from the *barhis* like a *prastara* and placed it in the clarified butter vessel, he covers it with a blade of grass and throws it into the fire.

(36) Then, having removed the yoke-pins (*śamyā*), he sprinkles water around [the fire] in the same manner. He completes the formulas with the words "Thou hast consented" (*anvamaṃsthāḥ*) and "Thou hast impelled" (*prāsāvīḥ*).
(37) Then, having drawn out the waters for the *praṇītā* from the quarters, he gives a cow to the Brahmins, saying, "I give a boon to the Brahman. (38)
This is the *dārvīhoma* of the *āghāra* offering.

39. Now, another [method]: having swept around [the fire], sprinkled water around it, strewn grass around it, melted the clarified butter (*ājya*), purified it, heated the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, wiped them, and taken four portions of butter into the *sruk*, he recites all the mantras together and offers the oblation all at once. 40.
Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is the second [deity]. 41.

"He offers twice, wipes [the ladle] twice, eats twice, moves away, sips water, and licks [the vessel]—this is the *āgnihotrika* method. Now, another way: having swept around, sprinkled water, and strewn grass, he offers oblations with ordinary sacrificial food (*havir*) as prescribed; this is the *apūrva* (novel) method. Regarding this, they cite: "Bādari says that the *āghāra* is the archetype (*prakṛti*) of the *darvīhoma*; likewise Ātreya says it is the *āgnihotrika*; but Kāśakṛtsna says it is the *apūrva*."
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the fifth chapter in the first book: One should not let it [the fire] touch another [fire] unless there is an instruction to that effect. 1.

He leads him toward this fire. Then he lifts her up from her father’s lap or the teacher’s, [reciting]: "The consumption-diseases which follow the bride’s bridal procession among the people—may the gods who belong to the sacrifice lead them back to whence they came.

(2–3) Then, taking her by the right hand and causing her to mount his own chariot, he leads her to his own home, [reciting]: "May Pūṣan lead you from here, grasping your hand; may the Aśvins carry you forward on their chariot. Go to the house so that you may become a mistress of the house; as such, may you speak with authority in the assembly. (4)
He recites over the path: "I have ascended the easy path, the uninjured one, which carries one safely; on it the hero is not harmed, and he acquires wealth from others.

(5) He recites over the plants, the trees, the rivers, and the forests: "The plants that exist, the trees that exist, the rivers that exist, the deserts that exist, and the forests that exist—may they, O bride, release you, who are rich in offspring, from distress. (6)

Then, having brought his wife, he causes her to enter his own house with the verse: "I enter the auspicious houses, well-disposed, not slaying heroes, rich in heroes, bringing nourishment and pouring forth clarity; in them may I lie down, well-disposed. (7) Then he makes her sit down upon the hide of a bull with the verse: "Here let cattle be born, here horses, here men; here let wealth with a thousand-fold sacrificial fee and abundance of food settle down. (8) At this point, the attendants cause the two of them to tread upon stalks of grain. (9)
Then, he restrains his speech until the rising of the stars.

(10) Then he addresses the junction of day and night with the mantra: "O dark-blue and red ones, you two are present; the attachment of the sorceress is revealed. May her kinsmen prosper; may her husband be bound in bonds.
(11) Then, when the stars have risen, having gone outside, he shows him the Pole Star and Arundhatī. (12)
"You are firm, you have a firm foundation; you are firm, established by the firm. You are the pillar of the constellations; as such, protect me from those who attack. Thus [he addresses] Dhruva.

"When the Seven Seers led Arundhatī to the first place among the Kṛttikās for the sake of stability—she who bears the primary conjunction with the six Kṛttikās—may this eighth one, Arundhatī, prosper for us. Thus [he addresses] Arundhatī.

Then, having performed the worship of Arundhatī for the sake of the wedding, he undertakes the vow: "O Agni, lord of vows, I shall perform the vow of the *upayamana*; may I be able to do so; may it be successful for me. "O Vāyu, lord of vows... O Āditya, lord of vows... O Lord of Vows of vows, I shall perform the vow of the *upayamana*; may I be able to do so; may it be successful for me.
(15) Both the husband and wife, performing the vow, become students of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*); they sleep on the ground.
(16) Between them stands a staff of *udumbara* wood, smeared with fragrant unguents and wrapped with a cloth or a cord, until the offering of the cooked oblation. (17)

On the fourth night, when the cooked oblation has been offered, he releases the vow and raises the staff with the mantra: "O Lord of the Forest, you have risen up from the strength of the earth; grow forth with a hundred branches! Speaking of food and strength through you, may we rejoice in the abundance of wealth and in nourishment.
(18) Then he hands it to the bride with the mantra: "I unite you with offspring, as one mixes *surā* with *māsara*.
(19) The bride receives it with the mantra: "May I be possessed of offspring. (20)

Then he hands it over to the bridegroom with the words: "I unite you with offspring and cattle, as one mixes *surā* with *māsara*. (21) The bridegroom accepts it with the words: "May I be rich in offspring and rich in cattle.
(22) Then, having placed it near the pillar, he approaches by way of the side. (23)

The lying down [of the bride] is well known. On the following day, having taken up the staff and having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made, he dismisses her into the waters.

Then, having performed the rites from the drawing of lines for the sacrificial ground for the gods up to the *agnimukha*, he offers oblations of cooked food with the two verses beginning, "Agni is the head of the world" (*agnirmūrdhā bhuvaḥ*).
The rite from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering until the bestowing of the cow as a gift is established.
This is the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha].
Then, after the sun has set, having adorned one another, they lie down on their upper beds.
Then he addresses the bride: "This bride is auspicious; come together and behold her. Having bestowed good fortune upon her, depart for your homes.

(30) Then he unites her with a garland fragrant with all kinds of perfumes: "May our minds be united, may our hearts be united, may our bodies be united. They unite you with the bond of desire so that you shall not be released.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the sixth chapter of the first book:
They bring this fire.
Then, having performed the rites from the marking of the sacrificial ground up to the carrying forward of the *praṇītā* waters, he asks for cooked rice or milk-rice for the footstep.
Having sprinkled it [with water], he places it on the fire;
he pours out the clarified butter;
then he places the clarified butter on the fire.
Having carried fire around both [the sacrificial pot and the implements], he cleans the stirring-spoon and the dipping-spoon.
(6) Then, having cooked this *caru* oblation, having sprinkled clarified butter over it, and having removed it from the fire toward the north, he pours butter over it once it has been set down.
(7) Having performed the rites from the laying of the enclosing sticks up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), he offers an oblation from the cooked portion. (8)
In this very manner, the procedure for the *caru* applies to all *sthālīpāka* offerings.

(9) Having recited the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*), "He who, honoring thee with a heart full of praise... (RV 10.61.7), he offers the oblation with the offering verse (*yājyā*), "To whichever righteous man, O Jātavedas... (RV 10.2.3).
(10) Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*). (11)

O Agni, you are the expiation among the gods; I, a Brahmin seeking protection, take refuge in you. Whatever body of hers is husband-slaying, child-slaying, cattle-slaying, or fortune-slaying—I render that body of hers [harmless] to the paramour; *svāhā*! O Vāyu, you are the expiation among the gods; I, a Brahmin seeking protection, take refuge in you. Whatever body of hers is husband-slaying, child-slaying, cattle-slaying, or fortune-slaying—I render that body of hers [harmless] to the paramour; *svāhā*!

"O Āditya, you are the expiation among the gods; I, a Brāhmaṇa seeking protection, take refuge in you. Whatever body in her is husband-slaying, offspring-slaying, cattle-slaying, or fortune-slaying—I render that [body] for her a slayer of paramours, svāhā!

(14) O Prajāpati, you are the expiation among the gods; I, a Brāhmaṇa seeking protection, take refuge in you. Whatever body in her is husband-slaying, offspring-slaying, cattle-slaying, or fortune-slaying—I render that [body] for her a slayer of paramours, svāhā!
(15) From the cooked [oblation] itself, the offering to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is performed with the two *sviṣṭavatī* verses. (16)
In the other case, [the offering] is with parched grains (lāja). 17.

"To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt—the bearer of oblations, the subduer of enemies, the slayer of Rākṣasas, the victor in battles, the luminous, the shining, the wise—we call for the well-offered sacrifice. O Agni, with the well-offered sacrifice, fulfill that; O God, overcome all hostile armies. Show us a wide path and shine forth; bestow upon us a long, undecaying life. Svāhā! 18.
The rite from the Jaya-oblation onwards is established as complete up to the granting of the boon of a cow. 19.
Then, having placed gold beneath it, he pours the remainder of the clarified butter as a libation upon her head, saying: "Bhūḥ svāhā! Bhuvaḥ svāhā! Suvaḥ svāhā! Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ svāhā!
(20) Then he leads her clockwise around the fire, saying: "May they quickly go around Aryaman’s fire; may the mother-in-law and the brothers-in-law look on with favor. (21)

Then, having prepared a splendid house—swept and smeared with cow dung, fragrant with scents, flowers, incense, and lamps, furnished with couches, well-perfumed, illuminated in all directions by lamps fed with ghee and cotton wicks, and provided with water-jars and mirrors at its head—and having laid her down upon it, he mutters [the mantra] in her presence. 22.

"Arise from here, O Viśvāvasu! We honor you with obeisance. Seek another passionate woman; unite your wife with her husband. Arise from here, for she has a husband; she honors Viśvāvasu with obeisance and songs. Seek another woman who sits among the fathers and is manifest; that is your portion by birth—know this! (23) Then he makes her lie down with the verse: "The glory of Prajāpati is in the woman. (24) Then he uncovers her womb with the formula: "For progeny, thee. (25)

If she should shed tears, he addresses her with the mantra: "Living, weeping, and moving about at the sacrifice, the men have envisioned a long-lasting lineage. A blessing to the fathers who have prepared this; joy for the husbands, as wives embrace. (26) Thus ends the sixth chapter of the first book in the Bodhāyana Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the seventh chapter of the first book.
One born of a Brāhmaṇa father and a Brāhmaṇī mother is designated as "born" (jāta) prior to initiation (upaneyana).
[1] One who has merely been initiated and observes the vows, having studied a small portion of the Vedas, is a Brāhmaṇa. [2] One who has studied a single recensional branch (śākhā) is a Śrotriya. [3]
One who has studied the auxiliary sciences (aṅga) is an *anūcāna*; 4. one who has studied the ritual manuals (kalpa) is an *ṛṣikalpa*; 5.
one who has studied the aphorisms (sūtra) and the sacred teachings (pravacana) is a *bhrūṇa*. 6.
The seer is one who has studied the four Vedas. 7.
From this point onward, [the child] is a god. 8.

Now, if he should desire, "May I procreate a learned scholar (śrotriya)," then, having performed the rites up to the worship of Arundhatī, the two [parents] shall remain for three nights as celibates (brahmacārins), eating food that is neither pungent nor salty, and sleeping on the ground. 9.
He shall wear unwashed garments and adorn himself with ornaments in the evening and the morning; he shall carry arrows and a goad, and perform service to the sacred fire.
On the fourth day, there is an oblation of cooked food and the ritual lying down together.
Now, if he should desire, "May I procreate those who do not know the Ṛgveda," he should observe this vow for twelve nights.
At the conclusion of the vow, there is an oblation of cooked food and sexual intercourse.

(13) Now, if he should desire, "May I produce one who is like a seer," he should observe this vow for a month. (14) At the conclusion of the vow, there is an oblation of cooked food and sexual intercourse. (15)
Now, if he should desire, "May I give birth to a bhrūṇa," he should observe this vow for four months. (16) At the conclusion of the vow, there is an offering of cooked food and cohabitation.
(17) Now, if he should desire, "May I give birth to a ṛṣi," he should observe this vow for six months. (18)
At the conclusion of the vow, there is an oblation of cooked food and lying down together.
(19) Now, if he should desire, "May I procreate a god," he should observe this vow for a year. (20) At the conclusion of the vow, there is an oblation of cooked food and lying down together. (21)

Now, when she has become one whose clothes are soiled with menstrual blood, he should not converse with her, nor sit with her, nor eat her food; for she stands there having assumed the form of the murder of a Brahmin (brahmahatyā). Moreover, they say: "Ointment indeed is a woman's food; ointment alone should not be accepted, but anything else may be taken at will. He should not approach her [for intercourse], nor in the forest.
He does not look backward; 25. he does not bathe; 26. he does not anoint himself. 27.
He does not scratch himself; 28.
he does not apply ointment; 29.
he does not clean his teeth. 30.
He does not clip his nails. 31. He does not cut [wool]. 32. He does not spin thread. 33.
He does not drink from a leaf.
He does not drink from a vessel that is curved at the top.

Regarding this, the Brāhmaṇa states: "For three nights she should observe a vow; she should drink either from her cupped hands or from a vessel that is not curved at the top, for the protection of her offspring."

On the fourth night, when she has bathed, having adorned her, he addresses her on the bed: "May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms. May Prajāpati pour [the seed]; may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you.
(37) As the earth has Agni as its embryo, as the sky is pregnant with Indra, as Vāyu is the embryo of the quarters—so may he place the embryo within you.
(38) Bestow an embryo, O Sinīvālī; bestow an embryo, O Sarasvatī. Bestow an embryo, O Aśvins, the two gods crowned with lotuses; may they place it [within you]. (39)"
The two fire-sticks from which the Aśvins churned the golden fire—that embryo I place within you, so that you may give birth in the tenth month.
40 O Nejameṣa, fly away; fly back again with a son. Bestow upon this woman who desires a son an embryo that shall be a male. 41

Then he embraces her with: "I am he; you are she. I am heaven; you are earth. I am the seed; you are the bearer of the seed. I am the mind; you are speech. I am the Sāman; you are the Ṛc. Come, let us two unite; let us both deposit the seed for the sake of obtaining a male son, for the increase of wealth, for good progeny, and for heroic vigor.

(42) He touches himself with: "I have deposited the embryo in the plants; I [have deposited it] within all beings. I have brought forth the offspring of the fathers; I [have brought forth] sons from women in the future. (43)

Then he approaches her with the verse: "O Pūṣan, make her most auspicious for us, she in whom men sow the seed; she who, longing for us, shall spread her thighs apart, so that we, longing for her, may strike our phallus into her.
(44) He approaches her in this very manner from the fourth night onwards, up to the sixteenth, each subsequent even-numbered night.
(45) "Approaching one's wife during her season leads to the highest good of progeny," so say the teachers. (46)

"Bodhāyana says that all acts of approaching [the teacher] are accompanied by mantras. Śālīki says it is only that which occurs at the beginning and that which occurs during the Ṛtu-rite. Thus ends the seventh chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now, in the first book, the eighth chapter.

Then, on the fifth day, they perform the barber’s work for these two. (1) Having given milk-rice to the barber, they go out from the village toward the east or the north direction; where they see the root of a single *udumbara* tree, having swept around it keeping it to their right, they cause [the barber] to anoint it with perfumes while reciting: "O Lord of the Forest, as you have risen up with vigor, O Lord of the Forest, may you grow forth with a hundred branches; even so may we grow forth with sons and cattle, with a thousand branches. (2)
"With *sumanas* flowers he covers [the tree], saying: 'O Lord of the Forest, as you are rich in fruit, so may I be rich in fruit through sons and cattle.
(3) Right there, he offers an oblation of threefold food.
(4) And they recite the mantra: 'O Lord of the Forest, full of vigor, full of milk, swelling with milk, turn toward us with milk! (5)"

Having prepared the food, honored the Brahmins, and caused them to pronounce blessings, he descends into water reaching up to his knees. With an unwashed garment having its fringes pointing eastward, he asks a student who is catching fish and inquiring, "Student, what do you see?
(6). Being thus questioned, he should reply, "Sons and cattle. (7).
Then, at the foot of an Udumbara tree, he offers these fish as a Bali-oblation for the cranes with the words, "For long life and for splendor. (8)
Right here, having fastened the floral remains (*nirmālya*), the worn garments, and the *pratisara* threads, and having tied them together upon a branch of the *udumbara* tree; 9.
Then, having plunged into the water and rubbed each other's backs, they go toward the water’s edge and separate, saying: "The noose of Varuṇa is unfastened; the noose of Varuṇa is cast away. 10.
Having adorned one another and put on red garments, [they do so] with the verse beginning, "With a new garment... 11.
Having gone home either by carriage or on foot, they wash their feet, sip water, and, remaining silent, begin the act of lying down.
(12) On the following day, he commences with the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice. (13) And during the dark fortnight, he performs it with the monthly *śrāddha*. (14)
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the ninth chapter in the first book: When pregnancy is recognized, the *puṃsavana* (rite for ensuring a male child) is performed under the asterism Tiṣya. 1.
Having served food to the Brahmins and caused them to recite, "An auspicious day! Welfare! Prosperity!", [he proceeds]. 2.

Then, having performed the rites from the marking of the sacrificial ground for the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha), he offers oblations of cooked food with the verse: "O Prajāpati, take pleasure in my body; O Tvaṣṭṛ, together with the gods, with Indra, and with all the gods, being in harmony with our protections, may we be mothers of many sons, svāhā!
3. Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter with three verses according to their meters, beginning: "He is the embryo of the plants, the embryo of the trees... 4.
The rite from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards is established up to the giving of the cow as a boon. 5.
Then he causes the remainder of the clarified butter to drip into her mouth with the four verses beginning with "O gods, look upon us for the sake of beauty," each according to its meter.
6. Thus ends the ninth chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyasūtra.
Now, the tenth chapter in the first book:
In the fourth month of the first pregnancy, the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) is performed.
Having served food to the Brāhmaṇas and having caused them to pronounce, "An auspicious day! Welfare! Prosperity! (puṇyāhaṃ svasti ṛddhiḥ).
Then, having performed the rites from the marking of the place for the sacrifice to the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (the oblation to Agni), he offers an oblation of cooked food.
Having recited the invitatory verse, "May Dhātṛ give to us," he offers with the offering verse, "Dhātṛ rules over progeny and wealth.
Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter, [reciting] from "May Dhātṛ give us wealth toward the east" until the end of the section.
The ritual from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards is established as usual, up to the presentation of the cow and the granting of the boon.

Then, with a porcupine quill from a weapon-bearing animal, using three tufts of *darbha* grass, *udumbara* flowers, and barley flowers, he parts her hair and raises the *sīmanta* (parting) while reciting the two verses: "O Rākā, worthy of honor... and "Thine [are] the honors... (RV 2.32.4–5).
Then he ties barley flowers to her head, saying: "Thou art barley; bar away our hatred, bar away our enemies. (RV 10.97.20).
Then he welcomes these two lute-players with the words, "Welcome! (9). Then he instructs them, "Sing!
(10). They sing this verse: "Soma alone is our king," so say the Brāhmaṇa subjects; "seated with wheels turned back, [we dwell] on this bank of yours. (11)
He utters the name of that river upon whose bank they dwell.
12. In the eighth month, he offers oblations to Viṣṇu with this hymn, "viṣṇornukam. 13.
He presents an offering to Viṣṇu. 14.
For this month is known as Vaiṣṇava;
for Viṣṇu is the deity of the embryo.
Thus has the Huta sacrifice been explained. 17.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the eleventh chapter of the first book: Regarding the offering of the bali-oblation after the fire has been kindled. 1.

For Viṣṇu, Bali [should sacrifice] on the seventh or twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the eighth month, under the asterism Rohiṇī or Śroṇā (Śravaṇā). Having served food to the Brāhmaṇas and caused them to pronounce, "An auspicious day! Well-being! Prosperity!", he then performs the rites from the marking of the sacrificial ground for the deity up to the pouring of the *praṇītā* water. Rising, he invokes the deity in front of the fire, saying: "Oṃ bhūḥ, I invoke Puruṣa; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I invoke Puruṣa; Oṃ suvaḥ, I invoke Puruṣa; Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ, I invoke Puruṣa. Having thus invoked him...
Having performed the rites from the putting on of the garments up to the invocation of the fire (agnimukha), he worships the deity.

(5) Having purified himself with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*, with the four verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*, and with this entire section (*anuvāka*) beginning with *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*; (6) he then satiates [the deities] with water, saying: "I satiate Keśava; I satiate Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana, Trivikrama, Vāmana, Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and Dāmodara. (7)
Having worshipped with these very names, using perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, saying "Homage to such-and-such! Homage to such-and-such! (8).
Then he offers oblations to Viṣṇu with [the verses]: "Viṣṇo nu kam," "Tadasya priyam," "Pratadviṣṇuḥ," and "Trirdevaḥ paromātrayā vicakrame" (9).
From the *jaya* offering onwards, the rite is established up to the granting of the boon by the cow (10).

Then he offers food consisting of milk-rice with jaggery mixed with ghee, saying twelve times according to the respective deities: "Svāhā to [Name], obeisance to [Name]; svāhā to [Name], obeisance to [Name].
(11) They praise him with Viṣṇu-related hymns from the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, using stotras and praises.
(12) Having caused the Puruṣa to depart with the Vyāhṛtis, saying, "I cause the Puruṣa to depart," he should have the wife eat the remainder of the food. (13)

"It is known that a male is born from her. (14) Thus ends the eleventh chapter of the first book in the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyasūtra. Regarding this: "Having announced [the event], one should offer the *arghya* water. Then, on a pure and level spot; then, having risen toward her; one should not let them touch each other. They bring this fire. [A son] produced by a Brāhmaṇa father and a Brāhmaṇī mother. Then, for these two, on the fifth day; when the pregnancy is recognized; in the fourth month of the first pregnancy. Just as this offering of the *bali* oblation is performed after the *homa* has been offered. (11)

As for this offering of oblations (*baliharaṇa*) when the fire has been established: in the fourth month of her first pregnancy, once pregnancy is known; then, on the fifth day thereafter, [the son] born of a Brāhmaṇa father from a Brāhmaṇa mother—[the father] brings this fire. He should not let it mingle with another fire. Then, having approached her, and then in a pure, level place, having announced [the occasion], he should offer the guest-water (*arghya*). As for this [matter]: 11. Thus ends the first book (*praśna*) of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyasūtra*. Now begins the first chapter of the second book.
Then, after the offering has been made: 1. He addresses the newborn boy with this Anuvāka beginning, "Born from the waters...
2. Then he bathes him with these six verses in their proper order, beginning, "For the field-disease thee, for Nirṛti thee... 3.
Then he places him upon his own lap with the verse: "From limb by limb you arise; from the heart you are born. You are indeed the self named son; live a hundred autumns!

(4) Then he smells him on the head with the formula: "Become a stone, become an axe, become unassailable gold. With the *hiṅkāra* of cattle, I smell you, O [Name]! using the name of the lunar mansion.
(5) Then he mutters into his right ear with the five sections beginning, "Agni is long-lived. (6)
Then, having mixed together curds, honey, and clarified butter, he makes him eat it with a piece of gold, verse by verse, with this Anuvāka beginning, "The breath protects all that moves.
(7) He pours the remainder into the footprint of a cow with the Vyāhṛtis.
(8) Then he places him on his mother's lap with the four verses beginning, "Sit thou upon the lap of this mother," accompanied by the Haṃsa-verses. (9)

He consecrates the breast with the mantra: "That breast of yours which is inexhaustible, which is refreshing, by which you nourish all desirable things—that treasure-yielding, wealth-finding, and liberal one, O Sarasvatī, let it suckle here alone.

(10) He consecrates the child while he is sucking with the mantra: "May Heaven protect your back; may Vāyu and the Aśvins protect your thighs; may Savitṛ protect the one who is sucking the breast; from the garment down to the lower robe, may Bṛhaspati and the Viśvedevas protect you from behind. (11)
Then he places a water-pot near his head with the mantra: "O waters, be watchful while [the others] sleep; drive away the Rākṣasas from here.

(12) Then, having performed the rites beginning with the smearing of the sacrificial ground for the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (the oblation to Agni), he offers an oblation of cooked food. Having recited the invitatory verse (*puro'nuvākyā*): "The gods follow Hari as he goes," he offers the oblation with the offering verse (*yājyā*): "Do not cut me off, O Death; do not slay me.
(13) Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the verses beginning "To him who desires immediately," until the end of the section. (14)
The ritual from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards is established up to the giving of the cow as a gift.

(15) Then, having bathed, clothed, and adorned either a pair of oxen or a pair of chariot horses, he carries them forward past the fire; in front of them, he places the remnants of the oblation upon *aśvattha* leaves with the mantra, "Obeisance to the piercing ones.

(16) Then, after the sun has set, he offers white mustard seeds mixed with grain-husks with his joined palms, verse by verse, with this entire section beginning, "Make thy strength wide-spreading like a net. (17)

Then, having mixed together boiled rice, sesame flour, and ghee, he places the remains of the oblation upon *aśvattha* leaves in a cow-pen, saying: "Homage, homage to the Non-Terrible and the Greatly Terrible!

(18) Then they scatter what remains in all directions, saying: "To Āveśinī, Vyaśrumukhī, Kutūhalinī, Ekastanī, Jṛmbhaṇī, Stambhanī, Mohanī, Kṛṣṇā, Viśākhā, Vimalā, and Brahmarātrī—these unfailing ones fall upon those who count their enemies. Homage, homage indeed to these Mothers! (19)
In this very manner, he performs the rites beginning with the *phalīkaraṇa* oblation morning and evening for ten nights.
(20) As long as the woman who has given birth has not risen, the food [of that household] is not fit to be eaten.
(21) On the tenth day, she rises. (22)
The naming ceremony takes place on the tenth or the twelfth day.

Having offered oblations with the *prājāpatya* hymn, having served food to the Brahmins, and having caused them to pronounce "An auspicious day!", "Well-being!", and "Success!", he bestows a name upon him.
It should consist of two syllables, four syllables, six syllables, or eight syllables.
[A name] beginning with a sonant and ending with a semivowel, and terminating in a long vowel or a final *s* (abhiniṣṭhāna), [is a name].
Or rather, that in which the prefix *su-* occurs is understood to be "firmly established" [as a name].
It should resemble a seer (*ṛṣi*) or resemble a deity.

Their names shall be exactly like those of their ancestors. (29) A maiden’s name shall consist of an uneven number of syllables. (30) [The formula is: "May there be well-being for such-and-such a person. (31)
Thus ends the first chapter in the second book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the second chapter in the second book:
In the fourth month, the ceremony of going out [of the house] takes place. 1.

Having served food to the Brahmins and caused them to recite, "An auspicious day! Well-being! Prosperity!", [he performs the rite]. 2. Then, having performed the rites from the marking of the sacrificial ground for the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha), he offers the Svastyātreya oblation.

3. "May the Aśvins and Bhaga grant us well-being; may the goddess Aditi, who is not of the ocean, grant us well-being; may the Asura Pūṣan grant us well-being; may Heaven and Earth with their beautiful light grant us well-being. 4.

For our well-being, we invoke Vāyu and Soma, who is the lord of the world’s prosperity; for our well-being, Bṛhaspati with his entire host; may the Ādityas be our protectors for our well-being. (5) May all the gods today be for our well-being, and Agni Vaiśvānara, the Vasu, for our well-being; may the divine Ṛbhus protect us for our well-being; may Rudra preserve us from distress for our well-being.
(6) Grant us well-being, O Mitra and Varuṇa; grant us well-being, O wealthy Pathyā Svasti; grant us well-being, O Indra and Agni; grant us well-being, O Aditi. (7)
May we follow the path like the sun and the moon; meeting again, may we be reunited with those who give and do not harm, while possessing full knowledge.

(8) May we ascend Tārkṣya, the bringer of well-being, whose wheel is uninjured, the great being among the birds of the gods, the slayer of Asuras, the friend of Indra, the one of vast glory in battles—just as one boards a ship.

(9) With hands joined in reverence, I take refuge in Aṃhomuc, the descendant of Aṅgiras, Gaya, Svastyātreya, and Tārkṣya in my mind. May there be well-being for us, and may fearlessness prevail in times of distress. (10)

"May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being; may Tārkṣya with uninjured wheels grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati grant us well-being"—with these eight verses, according to their meters (11).
The rite from the *jaya* offering onwards is established as being completed up to the gift of the cow and the granting of the boon (12).

Then, having gone outside and worshipped the auspicious external objects, having honored the Brahmins with threefold food, having caused them to pronounce blessings, and having circumambulated [the fire], he leads them back to his own house (13).
Thus ends the second chapter in the second book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the third chapter in the second book:
In the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) takes place. 1.

Having served food to the Brāhmaṇas and caused them to recite, "An auspicious day! Welfare! Prosperity!", [he proceeds]. 2. Then, having performed the rites from the marking of the sacrificial ground for the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha), he offers oblations with the *Annasūkta* using the eight verses beginning with "I am the first-born of Cosmic Order," in accordance with their meters. 3.
The rite is completed with the *jaya* offerings and so forth, up to the gift of the cow and the granting of the boon. 4.

Then, having mixed boiled rice with curds, honey, ghee, and water, he makes the boy eat of the medicinal herbs with gold, using the six verses beginning with "The medicinal herbs that have been born," each according to its meter (5). With the formula, "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! I make thee eat the essence of the waters and of the medicinal herbs; may the waters and the medicinal herbs be auspicious for thee, O [Name]! he attaches this to every verse (6).
Thus ends the third chapter in the second book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the fourth chapter of the second book.
The tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākarma*) takes place in the first year, or after three years.
Having served food to the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce, "An auspicious day! Well-being! Prosperity! (2).

Then, having performed the rites from the marking of the place for the sacrifice to the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha), he offers oblations of cooked food. Having recited the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*) beginning with "ye keśinaḥ," he offers the oblation with the offering verse (*yājyā*) beginning with "narte brahmaṇaḥ. 3.

Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*), reciting the section beginning with "āroha proṣṭhaṃ viṣahasva śatrūn" until its conclusion. 4. From the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the ritual is established as standard until the gift of the cow and the granting of the boon. 5.
Then, in front of the fire, he places the remnants of the oblation upon udumbara leaves with the verse: "Homage to him who has golden arms... (VS 16.20).
To the west of the fire, he pours together two kinds of water.
He pours cold water into the hot water with the mantra: "O Vāyu, come with warm water; may Aditi shave the hair. (VS 16.21–22).
With these [waters] he moistens his head, saying: "May the waters moisten him for life, for long life, and for splendor.
(9) He raises up a blade of sacrificial grass with its tip pointing upwards, saying: "O herb, protect him!
(10) He consecrates the razor, saying: "So that he may long behold the sun! (11)
Then he places it [the razor] across him with the words: "O axe, do not harm him! (12).
Then he shaves his hair with the verse: "With that razor wherewith Savitṛ shaved [the head of]...
(13). As he is shaving, he addresses him with the mantra: "May this luster not depart following after thy hair. (14)
Then, having gathered them together, he places them upon a bunch of darbha grass with the words: "They chose for themselves many kinds of deposits.
(15) Then he immerses it in warm water with the words: "May Savitṛ bestow strength upon your two arms.
(16) Then he [wears it] with one crest, three crests, or five crests, according to whatever may be the family custom of these [students]. (17)
Some say that he should place the tuft of hair according to the specific Ṛṣi [of the family]. 18.
Then, having bathed him, clothed him, and adorned him, and having honored the Brāhmaṇas with food prepared from three-fold grain, he causes them to pronounce blessings. 19.
Thus the *prahuta* sacrifice is explained. 20.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the second book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the fifth chapter in the second book:
Next, the *āhuta* [offering]. 1.
One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception, a Rājanya in the eleventh year from conception, and a Vaiśya in the twelfth year from conception.
For a Brāhmaṇa, the time limit does not expire until the sixteenth year;
likewise for the other two, it is the twenty-second and the twenty-fourth years respectively.

Furthermore, there are optional rites: in the seventh [month] for one desiring Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasa*), in the eighth for one desiring long life, in the ninth for one desiring splendor, in the tenth for one desiring food, in the eleventh for one desiring sensory power, in the twelfth for one desiring cattle, in the thirteenth for one desiring intelligence, in the fourteenth for one desiring prosperity, in the fifteenth for one who has rivals, and in the sixteenth for one desiring all things. One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the spring, a Rājanya in the summer, a Vaiśya in the autumn, and a Rathakāra in the rainy season; or indeed, all of them in the spring.

Having served food to the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce, "An auspicious day! Welfare! Prosperity!", and having fed the boy, he shaves his hair silently as in the *caula* ceremony. Once the boy has bathed, is dressed in clean garments, and has tied his topknot, [the teacher] puts on the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) while reciting: "The sacred thread is the supreme purifier, that which was born together with Prajāpati in the beginning; put on this bright, life-prolonging, foremost sacred thread—may there be strength and splendor for you.
(7) Having caused the one wearing the sacred thread to sip water, he then leads him to the place of sacrifice. (8)

Then, having performed the rites from the marking of the place for the sacrifice to the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha), he causes [the student] to place a fuel-stick of *pālāśa* wood, anointed with clarified butter, onto the fire while reciting: "O Agni, god who grants life, being praised as one who reaches old age, whose face is ghee and whose back is ghee; drinking the ghee and the lovely nectar of the cow, lead this boy to old age like a father his son—svāhā!

(9) Then, having made him stand up, he makes him step upon a stone to the north of the fire with his right foot, saying: "Step upon this stone; like a stone, may you be firm. Tread upon those who attack you; overcome those who seek to fight you. (10)

Then, while causing him to put on the garment that has been freshly spun and woven under the asterism Tiṣya, he makes him recite: "The goddesses who spun, those who wove, those who stretched [the warp], and those who gave the borders on both sides—may those goddesses clothe you with old age; long-lived, put on this garment. (11)

He consecrates the garment as it is being put on: "Put it on! Clothe him with this garment; make him live for a hundred years, grant him long life. Bṛhaspati gave this garment to King Soma that he might put it on. Go to old age; put on the garment. Become a protector against the curses of the people. Live for a hundred autumns, full of luster; clothe yourself in the increase of wealth. Put this garment around you for well-being; become a protector against the curses of your kin. Live for a hundred long autumns, and while living, distribute riches among the worthy. (12)

Then, while winding a triple-stranded girdle of muñja grass three times around him from left to right, he causes him to recite: "The girdle of the Brāhmaṇa is made of muñja grass; that of the Rājanya is a bowstring; that of the Vaiśya is a woolen thread—or indeed, for all, it may be of muñja grass. 'This girdle has come to us, warding off ill-spoken words, purifying our protection and refuge, bringing strength through out-breath and in-breath, dear to the gods and auspicious. (13)

He addresses the one who has girt himself with the cord: "The guardian of the settled, the furthest limit of austerity, striking down the *rakṣases* and overcoming the enemies—do thou surround us on every side with auspiciousness. O girdle, may we not come to harm through thee as our supporter.
(14) He makes a knot at the region of the navel: "Thou art the knot of the vital breaths; do thou not loosen from me. (15)

Then, while fastening the skin upon him, he causes him to recite: "The black antelope skin for a Brāhmaṇa; the Ruru deer skin for a Rājanya; the goat skin for a Vaiśya; or indeed, the black antelope skin for all. 'The eye of Mitra, the supporter, more powerful, resplendent, glorious, enduring, kindled; an unwearied garment, ageless—this skin, O prize-winner, do I put on. (16)

Then he hands him a staff: one made of *pālāśa* or *bilva* wood for a Brāhmaṇa; one from a branch of a *nyagrodha* tree, with the tip pointing downward, or one of *rauhītaka* wood for a Rājanya; one of *vādara* or *audumbara* wood for a Vaiśya; or for all of them, one made of wood. "For you are Soma; make me a drinker of Soma"—with these words, [he takes] the *pālāśa* staff. "You are the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*); for the sake of the splendor of sacred knowledge, I take you"—with these words, [he takes] the *bilva* staff.
"O eye, place the eye in me"—with these words, [he takes] a fruit of the Nyagrodha tree.

(20) "O strength, you are strength; place strength in me"—with these words, [he takes] a fruit of the Rohītaka tree. (21) "O nourishment, you are nourishment; place nourishment in me"—with these words, [he takes] a fruit of the Bādara tree. (22)
"Thou art strength; bestow strength upon me"—with these words [he takes] one made of *udumbara* wood.

(23) "I am the shaker of the tree; my fame is like the ridge of a mountain. With my purifier held aloft, like a prize-winning steed, I am my own immortal essence—wealth together with splendor"—with these words [he takes] one made of wood. (24) "What is your name? "I am so-and-so"—this is the teaching of Śāṭhyāyana. (25)

Then he takes him by the right hand with the formula: "In whom the past and the future, and all worlds are contained; with him I take you for myself; I take you for myself; by Prajāpati I take you for myself, O [Name]!
(26) Then he entrusts him to the deities with the formula: "I entrust you to the gods; I entrust you to the Viśvedevas; I entrust you to all the gods; I entrust you to all the deities, O [Name]! (27)
Then he initiates him with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I initiate you, O [Name]!

(28) Then the boy offers an oblation of cooked food with the verse: "He who is the bull of the meters, omniform, who arose from the meters and from the Truth—may Indra endow him with wisdom; O God, may I become a bearer of the immortal Truth, Svāhā!
(29) Then he offers supplementary oblations of clarified butter with six verses according to their respective meters, beginning with: "For Kṣetrī, for thee; for Nirṛti, for thee. (60)

In this very manner, having offered oblations with the *Brahmasūkta* and with the six verses beginning with "brahmajajñānam," [the rite] from the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards is completed up to the granting of the boon of a cow. In front of the fire, he places the remnants of the oblation upon *palāśa* leaves with the mantra: "Homage be to Nīlagrīva and Vāyu."
Herein is the Sāvitrivrata. 34.

Then, having caused [the student] to place four fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood—moist, with their leaves and sprouts intact, a span in length, with unwithered tips, and smeared with clarified butter—he causes him to recite [the formula], or [sticks] from any one of the trees used for sacrifice. 35.
"O Agni, lord of vows, I shall perform the Sāvitra vow; may I be able to do it, may it be successful for me, svāhā! 36.
"O Vāyu, lord of vows! O Āditya, observer of vows! O lord of vows among vows! I shall perform the vow of Savitṛ; may I be capable of it, may it be successful for me, svāhā!

(37) Having placed a grass-bundle (kūrca) with its tip pointing north behind the fire, the teacher sits upon it facing east, [saying]: "Thou art the supporter of the kingdom, the teacher's seat; may I not forsake thee.
(38) In front of that, the boy, sitting on Darbha grass facing west and grasping the teacher's feet, says: "Sir, recite the Sāvitrī to me! (39)

Therefore, he begins with the words "Then the after-offering," and recites that verse, "That most excellent splendor of Savitṛ," first foot by foot, then half-verse by half-verse, and then the whole; likewise, he recites the *vyāhṛtis* separately at the beginning or end of the feet, and similarly at the ends of the two half-verses, and finally the entire verse.

(40) Then the boy, taking from the cooked food, eats it with the mantra: "May my body be observant; may my tongue be most sweet; may I hear much with my ears; you are the treasury of the Veda, covered by wisdom; protect what I have heard.
(41) Now, some say that one should eat before the *sāvitrī*, asserting that "food is indeed the Veda. (42)

One should not do it in that manner; rather, one should not eat until the Sāvitrī has been recited. Regarding this, the Śāṭhyāyana school states: "One should eat once the Sāvitrī has been recited, once it has been recited. 43.

Then, having touched water, he worships the sun with the *jyotiṣmatī* verse: "Upwards from the darkness... (RV 7.89.2). 44. Then he instructs him: "O student, eat your food, perform your duties, do not sleep during the day, tend the sacred fuel, go on your alms-round, always bring firewood from the forest, bring a water-pot, remain under the authority of your teacher, and study the Veda. 45.
He indeed does all this in that very manner. 46.
Then, handing him an unfilled bowl, he says: "Beg first from your mother. 47.
He should beg from his mother first. 48.
"O lady, give alms," thus should a Brāhmaṇa beg.
"O lady, give alms," thus should a Rājanya beg. "Give alms, O lady," thus should a Vaiśya beg.
Having collected that, he says to the teacher, "This is alms-food.
The other accepts it, saying, "This is good alms-food.

To the north of the fire, having fashioned two female effigies and having adorned them with perfumes and garlands, he honors the Brahmins with threefold food and causes them to pronounce blessings, saying, "May Faith and Intelligence be dear to you."
For three days they maintain this fire, avoiding alkaline substances and salt, and sleeping on the ground. 55.
In this very fire, one should offer fuel sticks in the evening and in the morning with the *vyāhṛti* formulas. 56.
Likewise always in another [fire] as well. 57.

Then he sweeps around the fire from left to right with the verse: "O Agni, accept our fuel today; shine forth, raising high the smoke of the sacrifice. Touch the celestial vault with your crest; extend yourself with the rays of the sun.

(58) Then he sprinkles water around the fire from left to right: to the south, eastward, with the formula, "O Aditi, grant your consent"; to the west, northward, with "O Anumati, grant your consent"; to the north, eastward, with "O Sarasvatī, grant your consent"; and all around from left to right, with "O God Savitṛ, impel [the sacrifice]. Or he may do so silently all around. (59)
In that [fire], he places fuel-sticks in the evening and in the morning with the *vyāhṛtis*: "bhūḥ svāhā, bhuvaḥ svāhā, suvaḥ svāhā, bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ svāhā.

(60) Having swept around it in the same manner and having sprinkled water around it in the same manner, he causes the ends of the mantras to meet with the words: "thou hast assented" (*anvamaṃsthāḥ*) and "thou hast impelled" (*prāsāvīḥ*).

(61) Then he worships it with three verses beginning, "O Agni, that splendor which is thine," and with three verses beginning, "In me be wisdom, in me progeny," according to this Brāhmaṇa passage: "Man is indeed divided sixfold. (62)
Then, when three nights have passed, taking this fire, they go toward that direction where its *palāśa* leaf is clearly visible.

He sweeps around it from left to right, saying: "O you of good fame, make me of good fame! As you are of good fame and renowned, so may I become of good fame and renowned; as you are of good fame and renowned, the guardian of the treasure of the gods, so may I become the guardian of the treasure of the Brahmins and of the Veda."

Having kindled the fire to the east or north of that [spot] and having strewn grass around it, he then offers two oblations for the expiation of a breach of the vow with the two verses: "Whatever flaw has occurred in my self, Agni has given sight back to me" (RV 10.127.1–2).

Then, while he causes [the student] to place four fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood—moist, with their leaves and shoots intact, a span in length, with tips not dried out, and anointed with clarified butter—or of any other tree suitable for sacrifice, he makes him recite:
"O Agni, lord of vows, I have performed the vow of Savitṛ; I was able to do it; may it be successful for me, svāhā! (TS 2.5.11.6).
"O Vāyu, lord of vows! O Āditya, lord of vows! O Lord of vows among vows! I have performed the vow of Savitṛ; I was able to do it; may it be successful for me, svāhā!
(68) Having likewise honored Suśravas and gratified the Brāhmaṇas with threefold food, he should cause them to pronounce blessings.
(69) At this point, some discard the staff, the deerskin, the girdle, and the garment. (70)

"Taking one after another, he takes his garment with the mantra: 'May all the gods rejoice after you, whose first garment we take away; may many brothers and friends follow you, the well-born one, as you grow.

(71) Then, having covered himself from below the navel to above the knees, wearing the staff, the deerskin, and the girdle, avoiding the *śrāddha* meal, impurity from birth or death, sexual intercourse, honey, and meat, subsisting on alms and sleeping on the ground, he goes to the house of the teacher (*ācārya*); for it is known that 'the teacher is indeed Brahman.
(72) Thus ends the fifth chapter of the second book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyasūtra*.
Now begins the sixth chapter of the second book.
It has been stated that one should bathe after having studied the Veda; this refers to the *samāvartana* (the return ceremony). 1.
They declare that the *veda* consists of the *mantra* and the *brāhmaṇa*. 2.
The name "Veda" applies to both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas.
(3) The Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas are the authority for the sacrifice.
(4) Having studied the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas, or having completed the observances. (5)
The difference is only this much. 6.

Now, having performed the rites from the marking of the place for the sacrifice to the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha), he anoints a fuel-stick of *palāśa* wood with clarified butter and places it on the fire at midday. 7.
That has been explained previously. 8.

Then he proceeds by merely shaving his hair, beard, body hair, and nails. Having performed [the rites] up to the taking of the umbrella as prescribed, he offers oblations of cooked food with [the verse]: "Bringing [fortune], spreading it out, making for herself a garment—clothing and cows, and always food and drink—bring that prosperity to me, together with woolly cattle, Svāhā!

(9) Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter with [the verses]: "May the students of sacred knowledge come to me, Svāhā! May I be glorious among the people, Svāhā! May I be better than the wealthy, Svāhā! O Bhaga, may I enter into you, Svāhā! O Bhaga, enter into me, Svāhā! (10)
The ritual from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards is established as usual, up to the giving of the cow and the granting of the boon.
(11) Then, in front of the fire, he places the remains of the oblation upon a *bilva* branch with the mantra: "O thousand-branched one, may I cleanse my sins in you; svāhā!

(12) Then, taking a portion from the cooked food, he eats it with the mantra: "As waters flow down a slope, as months follow the year, so may the students of sacred knowledge come to me from all sides; O Ordainer, svāhā! (13)
Having consumed [the food] and sipped water, he touches his own chest with the formula: "Thou art the neighbor; protect me; do not desert me.
(14) He remains right there until the rising of the stars.
(15) Then, when the stars have risen, having gone outside, he worships the quarters of the sky; from this point onward, the procedure is established as standard. (16)

In that fire into which one leads [the student], in that [fire] the studentship (*brahmacarya*) is performed, in that the observance of vows (*vratacarya*) is performed, in that the return ceremony (*samāvartana*) is performed, in that the taking of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*) is performed, and in that the domestic rites (*gṛhyāni karmāṇi*) are carried out.
