17. In that [fire] the optional rites (*kāmyāni*) are performed; in that the consecrations of offspring (*prajāsaṃskārāḥ*) are performed, so say some. 18. This very [fire], from the initiation (*upanayana*) onwards, is offered with the *vyāhṛtis* and fuel-sticks until the return ceremony. 19.
From the time of the *samāvartana* (the student's return home) until the taking of the hand in marriage, he offers oblations with clarified butter (*ājya*) accompanied by the *vyāhṛtis*.

(20) From the time of the taking of the hand in marriage, he offers these two oblations with his hand using either rice or barley: "To Agni, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! in the evening; and likewise in the morning: "To Sūrya, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā!
(21) Or he may offer with any one of the sacrificial materials used for the *agnihotra*. (22)

At every festival (parvan), there is a cooked oblation (sthālīpāka) for Agni. This [oblation] may be accompanied by the *āghāra* libations, or it may be like the *agnihotra*, or it may be a first-time offering (*āpūrvika*). With that [oblation], one should feed a learned Brāhmaṇa who has prepared the clarified butter.
Some say that one should give a bull to that person who has been most honored by him.

(26) Now, the procurement [of materials] for the one who has followed [the deceased] is according to his own social status. (27) When someone has followed [the deceased], there shall be a fast for either the wife or the husband. (28)

Or he may offer a single oblation with the verse: "O Agni, you are the unerring one, free from curses; you are indeed truth, you are the unerring one. Held by an unerring mind, carry the oblation with an unerring [mind]; grant us healing medicine, Svāhā! (29). The *āhuti* has been explained (30).
Thus ends the sixth chapter of the second book in the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the seventh chapter of the second book.
Now, regarding the Śūlagava sacrifice: it should be performed every year on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, or else under the constellation Ārdrā. 1–2.

When the cows are distressed or when the cows are protected, having kindled the fire in the forest and strewn it around, and having performed the rites up to the *praṇītā* waters, he takes sacrificial grass and dedicates the cow with the formula: "I dedicate you, acceptable to Īśāna.
According to some, [he does so] silently.
Then he sprinkles it with water, saying, "I sprinkle thee, acceptable to Īśāna.
Some say [he does so] silently.
They cause it to be slaughtered right there, with its head toward the west and its feet toward the north.
9. For her, once she has been consecrated, he performs an aspersion with water.
10. He silently causes her vital breaths to swell.
11. Having silently extracted the omentum, he takes out the heart.
And they prepare the avadānas (portions of meat).
12. Having placed them upon those very spits, they cook them over that same fire.
13. Then, having removed these from the spits, they cook them again in a pot. 14.
Then, having removed these [portions] after they have been sprinkled with clarified butter, he sprinkles the established [oblation].

(15) Having performed the rites from the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), he invokes the deity: "May the bay horses, harmonious in mind, bring thee hither with white steeds, accompanied by banners, swift as the wind, powerful, and fleet as thought; come quickly for my oblation, O Śarva!

(16) Then, with the *sruva* spoon, he offers the omentum (*vapā*), which has been spread out and sprinkled with clarified butter, after reciting the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*): "By the thousands, in thousands... and offering it with the sacrificial verse (*yājyā*): "Thee, the Lord of beings, the glory of all. (17)

Then, having mixed these portions—the heart, the tongue, the left foreleg, the right shoulder-blade, the left shoulder-blade, the rectum, the anus, the left thigh, the right thigh, the tail, and the head—with boiled rice, meat, and broth in the *iḍā-sūna* vessel, he offers them by dipping with the stirring-ladle (*mekṣaṇa*) into the eastern half [of the fire], saying: "To the god Bhava, svāhā! To the god Śarva, svāhā! To the god Īśāna, svāhā! To the god Paśupati, svāhā! To the god Rudra, svāhā! To the god Ugra, svāhā! To the god Mīma, svāhā! To the great god, svāhā! (18)

Then he offers in the middle: "To the wife of the god Bhava, svāhā! To the wife of the god Śarva, svāhā! To the wife of the god Īśāna, svāhā! To the wife of the god Paśupati, svāhā! To the wife of the god Rudra, svāhā! To the wife of the god Ugra, svāhā! To the wife of the great god, svāhā! (19)

Then, in the latter half [of the oblation], he offers: "Svāhā to the son of the god Bhava; svāhā to the son of the god Śarva; svāhā to the son of the god Īśāna; svāhā to the son of the god Paśupati; svāhā to the son of the god Rudra; svāhā to the son of the god Ugra; svāhā to the son of the god Bhīma; svāhā to the son of the great god. (19) Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter with the hymn beginning, "Salutation to your wrath, O Rudra," until the end of the section. From the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the ritual is established as usual, up to the granting of the boon and the presentation of the cow. (22)

Then, in front of the fire, he places the remains of the oblation upon Arka leaves with the mantra: "To that Rudra who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who is in the plants, and who has entered all beings—to that Rudra let there be homage.

(23) Having poured together the rinsings of the cooking pot, the remainder of the clarified butter, and the remainder of the water into a vessel, he sprinkles them while walking three times around the cows from left to right with a branch of cane, reciting the hymn beginning: "The cows have come home; they have made the sound 'bhadi'. (24) This is called the "Great Auspicious Rite" (*mahatsvastyayana*). (25)
Now, if he does not obtain a cow, he sacrifices a ram or a goat.
Or they cook a *sthālīpāka* for Īśāna; therefore, he performs everything that would have been done with a cow.
The *śūlagava* has been explained.
In exactly the same way, this much alone is different [in the case] of the eighth [lunar day] at nightfall. (29) There is no introductory rite for the animal sacrifice here.
(30) Thus ends the seventh chapter in the second book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now, the eighth chapter in the second book: Now follows the offering of the bali-oblation. 1.
Whether it be evening or morning, the oblation of whatever food is to be eaten should be performed either on the domestic fire (aupāsana) or on the cooking fire (pacana). 2.
The difference is only this much: 3. However, they prescribe an oblation for food that has been mixed with alkaline salt or inferior food. 4.
This may be done at will in other sacrificial sites. 5.
Now, if it should be only this [single fire], one should draw out embers mixed with ashes from the north and offer the oblation upon them.
(6) Having swept around all the sacrificial sites with the hand, one should perform the sprinkling of water on both sides.
(7) There is a repetition of the place and a repetition of the mantra; however, this may be done at will when the locations are identical. (8)

The oblation is performed with the hand, taking [the material] portion by portion: *svāhā* to Agni; *svāhā* to Soma; *svāhā* to Dhruva; *svāhā* to Dhruva-bhūma; *svāhā* to Dhruvakṣiti; *svāhā* to Acyutakṣiti; *svāhā* to Īśāna; *svāhā* to Jayanta; *svāhā* to Dharmaruci; *svāhā* to Dhanvantari; *svāhā* to Vidyā; *svāhā* to Ambikā; *svāhā* to Hari; *svāhā* to the Gaṇas; *svāhā* to the Gaṇapatis; *svāhā* to the Councils (*pariṣad*); *svāhā* to the Viśvedevas; *svāhā* to the Sādhyas.
To all the gods, svāhā! To all the deities, svāhā! Bhūḥ svāhā! Bhuvaḥ svāhā! Suvaḥ svāhā! Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ svāhā!
(9) To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā—thus in the eastern part of the northern half.
(10) Behind the fire, [he offers] to Dharma, svāhā; to Adharma, svāhā. (11)
In front of the fire, [he offers] to Kadru with the words: "To Nākamātṛ, svāhā! To the serpents, svāhā! (12).

In the space near the spade, [he offers] to Avalā Devī with the words: "To Vāstupālī with her retinue, svāhā! (13). In the place near the spade, [he offers] to the Waters with the words: "To Varuṇa, svāhā! (14).
With the cooking pot [he offers], saying: "To Prajāpati, svāhā! To Parameṣṭhin, svāhā! (15).
In the space for the deities, saying: "To Ṛṣabha, svāhā! To Rudra, svāhā! To Rudrāṇī, svāhā! (16).
In the middle of the house, saying: "To the plants and trees, svāhā! To the Rakṣas and the divine folk, svāhā! (17).
"To the head, for desire, svāhā! To Bhaga, svāhā! To Śrī, svāhā! To Viṣṇu, svāhā! (18).
At the location of the pillar: "To the house, svāhā! To the king of the house, svāhā! (19).
In the space above the wealth and grain: "To wealth and grain, svāhā! To Vaiśravaṇa, svāhā! (20).
"In the cow-pen or in the pond, svāhā to Śrī! Svāhā to Puṣṭi! (21).
"In the space between the mortar and pestle, svāhā to the mortar and pestle! (22).
"In the space between the lower and upper grinding stones, svāhā to the lower and upper grinding stones! (23).
In the space for the Samūhanī, [he offers] with: "To the goddess Samūhanī, svāhā! (24).

In the north-eastern part of the house, [he offers] with: "To the household deities, svāhā! To the dwellings, svāhā! To the lords of the dwellings, svāhā! To the serpent-deities, svāhā! To all beings, svāhā! (25).
In the middle of the door, [he offers] with: "To the intermediate space, svāhā! To the lower intermediate space, svāhā! (26).

On the two sides: "To the Creator, svāhā! To the Ordainer, svāhā! (27). On the two upper sides: "To Prosperity, svāhā! To Abundance, svāhā! (28). At the place of the enclosure: "Whatever moves and whatever stirs in the world—this is a portion of Name; to Name, svāhā! (29).

Then, having gone outside, [he offers] at the opening for the *jyeṣṭhā* (the upper hole): "To the two *jyeṣṭhās*, svāhā!"; at the opening for the *karaskara* (the lower hole): "To the two *karaskaras*, svāhā! (30). On the cart or on the chariot, [he offers]: "To Śrī, svāhā! To Viṣṇu, svāhā! (31). In the cow-pen, [he offers]: "To Rudra, svāhā! To the cattle, svāhā! To Paśupati, svāhā! (32).

To Vāstoṣpati in the midst of the dwelling, Svāhā! To the Earth, Svāhā! To the Atmosphere, Svāhā! To the Sky, Svāhā! To Sūrya, Svāhā! To Candramas, Svāhā! To the Nakṣatras, Svāhā! To the Waters, Svāhā! To the Herbs, Svāhā! To the Forest Trees, Svāhā! To the moving and unmoving, Svāhā! To the gliding creatures, Svāhā! To the reptiles, Svāhā! To the regions, Svāhā! To the times, Svāhā! To the worlds, Svāhā! To the gods, Svāhā! To the Ṛṣis, Svāhā! To the Vasus, Svāhā! To the Rudras, Svāhā!
"To the Ādityas, svāhā! To Indra, svāhā! To Bṛhaspati, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! To Brahman, svāhā!

(33) Then, on the south side, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he says: "To the ancestors, svadhā! Adoration, svāhā! To the grandfathers, svadhā! Adoration, svāhā! To the great-grandfathers, svadhā! Adoration, svāhā!
(34) Then, having touched water, on the north side, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), he says: "Adoration to the blessed Rudra, svāhā! (35)

Then, for the cardinal directions: "Hail to the eastern direction! Hail to the southern direction! Hail to the western direction! Hail to the northern direction! Hail to the upward direction! Hail to the downward direction! (36) Then, for the intermediate directions: "Hail to Yama! Hail to Nirṛti! Hail to the Rākṣasas! Hail to Īśāna! (37) Then he tosses [the offering] into the air: "Those beings who roam by day, seeking the offering, the servants of Vituda—to them I bring the offering, desiring prosperity. May the Lord of Prosperity bestow prosperity upon me, Svāhā! Thus during the day. (38)

"Whatever beings roam about at night, seeking the offering, the servants of Vituda—to them I bring the offering, desiring prosperity; may the Lord of Prosperity bestow prosperity upon me, svāhā!"—thus at night.
(39) He pours out the rinsing water in the north-eastern direction, saying: "Homage to Rudra who dwells on the earth, svāhā!
(40) Thus ends the eighth chapter in the second book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the ninth chapter of the second book.
Having performed the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, one should wait for a guest until the time of milking the cows; or, having set aside the first portion, one should give it [to the guest]. 1–2.
It is known that this fifth sacrifice is the guest.

Having sat down behind the Gārhapatya fire, or behind the Upāsana fire, and having addressed the Gārhapatya with the words "Recite, sir!", he should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) and repeat the Sāvitrī one thousand times, or a hundred times, or an unlimited number of times, but not less than ten.

One should study the Vedas and the other sacred texts (*chandas*), as well as the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* hymns: "I praise Agni, the domestic priest" for the Ṛgveda; "For food thee, for strength thee" for the Yajurveda; "O Agni, come for the feast" for the Sāmaveda; "May the goddesses be auspicious for our aid" for the Atharvaveda; "Agni is the head of the world" for the *Chandas*; and "Whatever offense against the gods we have committed" for the *Kūṣmāṇḍas*. (5)

That which one studies is the sacrifice to Brahman; that which one offers oblations is the sacrifice to the gods; that which one offers the *svadhā* to the ancestors is the sacrifice to the ancestors; that which one brings the *bali* offering to the beings is the sacrifice to the beings; and that which one gives food to the Brahmins is the sacrifice to men.
(6) These five great sacrifices, when constantly and properly performed, lead one to the supreme goal.
(7) If even one of these five sacrifices is omitted by anyone, an oblation with the *manasvatī* verse is prescribed there as an expiation. (8)
If, however, through negligence, these have not been performed for two or three days, one should offer three *tantumatī* oblations and recite four *vāruṇī* verses.
(9) But if they have been entirely discontinued for ten or twelve days, one should offer four *abhyāvartinī* oblations and perform the *tāntumata* sacrificial pap (*caru*).
(10) In whose house a woman or an unmarried man should carry away these offerings, there the *Kūśmāṇḍī* verses are to be offered; having offered them, [one attains] the success of the sacrifice. (11)

He who has no one at home to perform these five great sacrifices when departing on a journey departs together with those sacrifices themselves. (12) While away from home, he should perform them if other food is available; if no food is obtained, he should complete them with water alone. (13) One should observe the vow with water according to what is available; by means of the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*), the twice-born attain equality with the gods. (14)

By the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), one [attains] the ancestors; by the sacrifice to the beings (bhūtayajña), the spirits (bhūti); by the sacrifice to men (manuṣyayajña), Manu; and by the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña), Brahman.
Having attained equality with these deities for a hundred years, they go to the bliss of Brahman—certain, eternal, and imperishable.

Now, a guest comes to him: either a forest-dweller (vaikhānasa) whose conduct is equal to that of his teacher, or a householder, or a forest-hermit (vānaprastha), or a wandering mendicant (parivrājaka), or one who has lost his fortune, or a bath-graduate (snātaka), or a king endowed with righteousness.
One should rise to meet them and offer them a seat, water for the feet, a respectful reception, or an offering of honor. 18.
Whatever medicinal herbs are available there should be given. 19. Or one may perform some other form of hospitality. 20.
One should offer a welcome to all who arrive, even down to dogs and Cāṇḍālas.
(21) However, the distribution of medicinal herbs should be performed by one who possesses wealth; in the absence of such means, [the offerings are] earth, water, grass, and kind speech.
(22) Indeed, these in the house of a virtuous man are never exhausted; therefore, they call these "the Supreme Brahman. (23)

Upon seizing them, however, there shall be a twelve-night period of eating food that is neither pungent nor salty, sleeping on the ground, and practicing celibacy. Having fasted for three nights, one may seize the two subsequent [sacrificial posts]. 25.
The offering of the *bali* is explained. 26.
Thus ends the ninth chapter of the second book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now, the tenth chapter in the second book:
Now follows the Pratyavarohaṇa (the ritual of descending).

Having offered oblations with the words, "Madhu and Mādhava, at the beginning of spring," and having adorned himself with spring ornaments and given spring foods to the Brāhmaṇas, he, together with his attendants, eats the remnants of the food.

Then, at the beginning of summer, having offered oblations with the mantra "Śukraśca Śuciśca," having adorned [the sacrificer] with summer ornaments, and having given summer foods to the Brahmins, he, together with his retinue, eats the remnants of the food. 3.

Then, at the beginning of the rainy season, having offered oblations with the mantra "Nabhaśca Nabhasyaśca," having adorned [the sacrificer] with rainy-season ornaments, and having given rainy-season foods to the Brahmins, he, together with his retinue, eats the remnants of the food. 4.

Then, at the beginning of autumn, having offered oblations with the verses "iṣaścorjaśca," and having adorned [the Brahmins] with autumnal ornaments and given autumnal foods to the Brahmins, he eats the remnants of the food together with his attendants. 5.

Then, at the beginning of winter, having offered oblations with the verses "sahaśca sahasyaśca," and having adorned [the Brahmins] with winter ornaments and given winter foods to the Brahmins, he eats the remnants of the food together with his attendants. 6.

Then, at the beginning of the Śiśira season, having offered oblations with the formulas "Tapaśca tapasyaśca," and having adorned [the sacrificer] with Śiśira ornaments and given Śiśira foods to the Brāhmaṇas, he eats the remnants of the food. 7. Now, during an intercalary month (adhimāsa), having offered oblations with the formula "Saṃsarpo 'si aṃhaspatyāya tvā," and having adorned [the sacrificer] with Caitra ornaments and given Caitra foods to the Brāhmaṇas, he eats the remnants of the food together with his attendants (sagaṇaḥ). 8.
This [rite] may be accompanied by the Āghāra libations, or it may be an Agnihotra rite, or even one involving the Āpūrvika offerings. 9.
The Pratyavarohaṇa has been explained. Thus ends the tenth chapter in the second book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the eleventh chapter in the second book.
Now follows the Aṣṭakā-homa. 1.
It should be performed on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Taiṣa. 2.
Likewise in Māgha, and likewise in Phālguna, if [the year] has been divided [into three]. 3.

If, however, the entire [rite] is performed later—on the seventh, eighth, or ninth day of the waning fortnight following the full moon of Mādhava—it may even be performed on the eighth day alone. [4] He invites the Brahmins, thinking, "I shall perform [the rite] tomorrow," [selecting those] who are related by birth, lineage, learning, and conduct, according to some. [5] One may invite them at will, even if they are relatives, provided they are endowed with learning and good conduct; for it is taught that the *svadhā* offering is deposited in learning and good conduct. [6]

On the following day, having honored them as best he can with the shaving of the beard, anointing, and bathing, and having himself bathed, he performs the rites beginning with the drawing of lines for the sacrifice to the gods on a pure and level spot, up to the preparation of the *praṇītā* water. Then, taking sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he dedicates the cow, saying: "I dedicate you, who are dear, to the fathers, to the grandfathers, and to the great-grandfathers. According to some, he does so silently. (7) Then he sprinkles it with water, saying: "I sprinkle you, who are dear, to the fathers, to the grandfathers, and to the great-grandfathers. According to some, he does so silently. (8)
They immolate it right here with its head turned westward and its feet toward the south.
(9) For it, once immolated, there is a sprinkling with water. (10) He causes its vital breaths to swell, silently. (11)
Having silently extracted the omentum, he takes out the heart (12).
And the prescribed portions are taken (13).
Having placed these upon those very spits, they cook them on that same fire (14).

They cook separate portions of meat, boiled rice, cakes, and other various kinds of food. When everything is prepared, he brings it all together and, having had an even number of Brahmins wash their hands and feet and perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), seats them on seats prepared with grass mats—two for the gods (*daiva*) and three for the ancestors (*pitrya*), or one for each of both groups—facing either east or north.
(15) If they face east, he ends the arrangement toward the south; if they face north, he ends the arrangement toward the east.
(16) Having poured water for them, he causes them to accept the invitation (*kṣaṇa*) while reciting the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*). (17)
At the Aṣṭakā-śrāddha, [the host says] "Please grant me your presence (kṣaṇaḥ kriyatām)," and the response is "Oṃ, so be it.
[18] "May you receive [it], may you receive [it]," [says the host].
[19] "I shall receive it, I shall receive it," the others reply. [20]
Then he causes them to accept water mixed with sesame seeds, saying: "Svadhā, obeisance to so-and-so; svadhā, obeisance to so-and-so.
(21) Some prescribe three offerings of water with sesame seeds: one before the food, two while they are eating, and the third when they have finished eating.

(22) Then, having honored them as best he can with garments, perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and garlands, he asks: "Let [the food] be served, and let it be offered in the fire. The others reply: "So be it. (23)
"Or rather, I shall perform [the offering] in the fire," he says; "Do so," the others reply.

(24) Then, being permitted, having performed the rites from the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) up to the *agnimukha* (the invocation of the fire), when the omentum (*vapā*) has been cooked, he offers five oblations with the *sruva*-ladle: "Those [waters] which flow toward the east, and those from the north—by means of these waters, the sustainers of the entire world, I place an interval between myself and my father. *Svadhā! Namas! Svāhā!* (25) I have placed an interval by means of the mountains, by the great earth, by the sky, by the infinite quarters, and by protective powers; I place an interval between myself and my grandfather. *Svadhā! Namas! Svāhā!* (26)"

I have placed an interval between [the deceased] and my great-grandfather by means of all the seasons, the days and nights with their junctions, and the half-months and months; *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*.
(27) Whatever of me my mother, acting without restraint, has caused to be lost while wandering—that seed may my father take up; let no other come near it; *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*.

(28) O Fathers, that limb of yours which the flesh-eating Jātavedas consumed when he led you forth to the worlds—that I now restore to you. Be whole with all your limbs, unharmed; *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*. (29)

Having divided the omentum into three parts, he offers it with a ladle made of Udumbara wood: "To him who is accompanied by the Pitṛs, the impetuous one, we offer this oblation. O Vāja, enjoy this our offering; you are self-born among the gods and the Pitṛs. Svadhā! Adoration! Svāhā!

(30) "I invoke Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases for our protection, and accompanied by the Pitṛs. O son of Vivasvat, eat this our offering; you are self-born among the gods and the Pitṛs. Svadhā! Adoration! Svāhā! (31)

"O Agni, carrier of the *kavya*, you who increase the cosmic order (*ṛta*), sacrifice to the ancestors; carry the oblation to the gods and the *svadhā* offering to the ancestors. To the gods and the ancestors, *svadhā*! Homage! *Svāhā*!

(32) Then he performs the *Aṣṭakā* oblation with fifteen verses beginning, "This is she who first shone forth," and one verse beginning, "Those who saw her before. And one verse beginning, "The image of the year"—these are seventeen. (33)

Then, having divided the cake into eight parts and offered three portions of the omentum according to the ritual procedure for the omentum, and having given the remaining portions to the Brahmins, he covers these sacrificial cuttings in the *iḍā*-troughs. Then, mixing the rice, meat, and broth together with clarified butter, he offers them in the southern half [of the fire] with a ladle made of *udumbara* wood, dipping it each time: "To the fathers, *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*! To the grandfathers, *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*! To the great-grandfathers, *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*! To the mothers, *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*!"

To the grandmothers, *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*. To the great-grandmothers, *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*. To the maternal grandfathers, *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*. To the maternal great-grandfathers, *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*. To the maternal great-great-grandfathers, *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*. To the maternal grandmothers, *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*. To the maternal great-grandmothers, *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*. To the maternal great-great-grandmothers, *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*. To the teacher, *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*. To the wives of the teachers, *svadhā*...

*Namaḥ svāhā! To the gurus, *svadhā namaḥ svāhā! To the wives of the gurus, *svadhā namaḥ svāhā! To the friends, *svadhā namaḥ svāhā! To the wives of the friends, *svadhā namaḥ svāhā! To the kinsmen, *svadhā namaḥ svāhā! To the wives of the kinsmen, *svadhā namaḥ svāhā! To the ministers, *svadhā namaḥ svāhā! To the wives of the ministers, *svadhā namaḥ svāhā! To all [ancestors], *svadhā namaḥ svāhā! To all [female ancestors], *svadhā namaḥ svāhā!* 34.
"To Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, svadhā, obeisance, svāhā!"—thus [he offers] in the eastern part of the southern half. 35.

Having placed rice with meat into the vessels, having added special ingredients, having mixed it with the remains of the oblation, and having set it down upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south, he covers it with *darbha* blades from the southern fire and touches it, saying: "The earth is your vessel, the sky is your lid; I offer you into the mouth of Brahman; I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; may you not fail for my fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers in yonder world, in that place. (36)
Then, having set these [foods] down before the Brahmins, he points them out with his thumb, without using the nail, saying: "To this one, *svadhā*! Homage! To that one, *svadhā*! Homage! (37).

He gazes at those who are eating with five [verses], beginning with: "I offer the nectar (*amṛta*) established in the vital breath (*prāṇa*). He gazes at himself with [the verse]: "O Brahmin woman, my self is for immortality. (38).
And from that point onward, he does not look about, for it is known: "The ancestors are bashful. (39).
Satisfying them with all desired objects and causing them to hear Vedic hymns accompanied by the *svadhā* invocation, as well as mantras that destroy Rākṣasas and those belonging to Nirṛti;

40. At the end of the satiation, having said, "Are you satisfied?", the reply is, "We are satisfied. 41. Having caused those who are satisfied to sip water, he scatters the remnants of the food into the receptacles with the verse: "May those born in my family who have been consumed by fire, and those who have not been consumed by fire, be satisfied by what is given on the ground; being satisfied, may they go to the supreme goal. 42.
Then, having sprinkled them with the rinsing water, having scattered [the remains], and having caused [them] to say "It is well-savored," he gratifies them with sacrificial fees. 43.
