The Vyāhṛtis accompanied by the Praṇava, breath control (prāṇāyāma), kindling the fire, begging for alms, standing, sitting, lying down, ritual ablution (upasparśana), and the offering of flowers—these are [the duties]. 23.

One should conclude [the rite] after enumerating as follows: "I satiate all the Sammita deities; I satiate Brahmā; I satiate Prajāpati; I satiate Parameṣṭhin; I satiate Sthāṇu; I satiate Śiva; I satiate Śarva; I satiate Bahurūpa; I satiate Skanda; I satiate Indra; I satiate Yama; I satiate the Ṛṣis; I satiate the Pitṛs; I satiate all the Sammita deities.
(24) One should behave toward those who act like a teacher in the same manner as toward a teacher. (25) When commanded, one should carry out exactly that, except in cases involving a mortal sin. (26)
In this manner, he should observe the vow for twelve years, or eleven, nine, seven, five, three, or two years; or for six months, four months, two months, or even one month.
Or alternatively, one who is learned in the Vedas and a *śrotriya* may observe the *parāka* vow for twelve nights; however, he must never be one who is unmeasured in his conduct.
He who performs this purifies ten ancestors, ten descendants, himself as the twenty-first, and the *paṅkti* (the assembly of five).
It purifies everything from whom he teaches, on whose seat he sits, to whom he gives, and from whom he receives.

(30) At the conclusion of his vows or at the completion of his Vedic study, a righteous man should offer a teacher’s fee according to his ability. (31) But if the teacher has fallen into distress, he may obtain it even from a fierce person or from a Śūdra. (32)

"From every quarter, even from a Śūdra, one may collect the materials for the sake of the teacher; this is righteous, so some say. (33) "By this [rule], the completion of the vows of other deities—such as those of Dhātṛ, Śiva, Bahurūpa, Pārṣada, Skanda, Indra, and Īśāna—is explained. One should practice the *brahma* (the Veda); whether it be Ṛg, Sāman, or Yajus, one should obtain the desire of the meters at each pressing (*anusavana*), so said Baudhāyana.
(34) Thus ends the third chapter in the third book of the Baudhāyanīya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the fourth chapter of the third book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*). During the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious constellation, having had his hair and beard shaved and having performed the introductory rite as before, he goes out from the village toward the east or the north. Having established the fire on a threshing-floor where no roof-covering is visible, having strewn grass around it, having placed the boiling water (*madantī*) over the fire, and having performed the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the first *anuvāka*, he prepares seats for the deities of the *pravargya* ceremony using *darbha* grass.
"To the east of the fire, I prepare for the Pravargya; I prepare for the Gharma; I prepare for the Mahāvīra; I prepare for the Sovereign.
(3) "To the south of the fire, I prepare for the Brahman; I prepare for Prajāpati.
(4) "To the north of the fire, I prepare for the Ṛṣis, the makers of mantras, the lords of mantras; I prepare for the gods who drink the Gharma. (5)

Then, on the south side, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he prepares [the portion] for the ancestors who drink the *agharma*: "I prepare for Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the ancestors.
(6) Then, having touched water, on the north side, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), he says: "I prepare for Rudra, whose priest is Rudra.

(7) Having sprinkled water around the fire from left to right and having placed fuel sticks of *vaikaṅkata* wood with the *vyāhṛtis*, he satiates the deities of the *pravargya* ceremony with the *madantī* waters. (8)
"To the east of the fire, I satisfy the Pravargya; I satisfy the Mahāvīra; I satisfy the Saṃrāj.
(9) "To the south of the fire, I satisfy the Brahman; I satisfy Prajāpati.
(10) "To the north of the fire, I satisfy the Ṛṣis, the composers of the mantras, the lords of the mantras; I satisfy the gods who drink the Gharma. (11)

Then, on the south side, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he says: "I satiate the ancestors who drink the Gharma; I satiate Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the Pitṛs. 12.

Then, having touched water, on the north side, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), he says: "I satiate Rudra, the Hotṛ of Rudra. 13. Then, having touched water, he says: "I satiate all the deities of the Pravargya. 14.

Then, while four fuel-sticks of Udumbara wood—whose tips are not dried out and which have been smeared with clarified butter—are being placed upon the fire, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite these mantras one by one: "The earth is the fuel," and so forth. 15.

Then he worships the deities: "O Agni, lord of vows, I shall perform the Śukriya vow; may I be able to do so; may it be successful for me. O Vāyu, lord of vows, I shall perform the Śukriya vow; may I be able to do so; may it be successful for me. O Āditya, lord of vows, I shall perform the Śukriya vow; may I be able to do so; may it be successful for me. O lord of vows, lord of all vows, I shall perform the Śukriya vow; may I be able to do so; may it be successful for me. (16) Then he causes [the student] to recite the beginnings of these sections, or those of the first and the last. (17)
Then he instructs him: "Having closed your eyes, restrain your speech.
(18) Then, with an unwashed garment, he wraps his head three times from left to right, including the face, saying: "You are piled up, you are well-piled up; svāhā! Be surrounded by the Maruts!

(19) Having sprinkled water around the fire from left to right and having placed fuel sticks of *vaikaṅkata* wood upon it with the *vyāhṛtis*, and having gratified the deities of the *pravargya* rite with the boiling water, he performs the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the final section (*anuvāka*). Then, before the sun has set, they go to the village. (20)
Restraining his speech, he should remain standing during this night, or he may sit down or lie down.

Then, in the morning when the sun has risen, having gone out from the village toward the east or the north, having established the fire on a threshing floor where no roof-covering is visible, having strewn grass around it, having placed the boiling water over the fire, and having performed the *śānti* rite with the first *anuvāka*, he prepares seats for the deities of the *pravargya* ceremony with *darbha* grass. Having loosened his garment with the verse "The birds, the fair-winged," he then points out six things to him: fire, water, the sun, a cow, a Brahmin, and gold.

Having first shown three [verses], and having shown the others as they occur, he should sprinkle water around the fire from left to right, place fuel-sticks of *vaikaṅkata* wood with the *vyāhṛtis*, satisfy the deities of the *pravargya* rite with the *madantī* waters, perform the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the final *anuvāka*, and then instruct him in the observance of his vows. 23.

He shall not mount a vehicle; he shall not climb a tree; he shall not descend into a well; he shall not hold an umbrella; he shall not wear shoes; he shall not sleep on a couch; he shall not converse with a woman nor with a Śūdra. If he must converse, he shall converse with a Brāhmaṇa. He shall not eat in the evening; if he eats in the evening, he shall eat only when the fire is kindled. He shall not bathe on the eighth day or on a festival day (parvan). On that day, however, he may bathe, but he shall remain standing and restrained in speech during that night, or he may sit or lie down. (24) Upon seeing impurity, blood, a corpse, or a vessel [containing such things], he shall look at the heavenly bodies. (25)

Upon seeing impurity, he mutters: "The mind is unbound, the eye is poor; the Sun is the best of lights. O Consecration, do not abandon me! (26). Now, if it rains upon him, he mutters in that instance: "Wetting [the earth], bestow strength! Bestow vigor! Bestow strength! Do not destroy my consecration or my fervor! (27).
He should observe this vow for a year, for the vow does not extend beyond a year; however, he may study this very [text] during that same year. (28)
If, however, he does not study during this year, he should observe this vow for as long as his study lasts; when the year has elapsed, he may then teach or cause [others] to hear it. 29.

Having performed the introductory rites as before, having gone out from the village toward the east or the north, having established the fire on a threshing floor where no roofs are visible, having strewn grass around it, having placed the boiling water over the fire, and having performed the *śānti* rite with the first *anuvāka*, he prepares seats for the deities of the *pravargya* ceremony with *darbha* grass; then he offers two oblations as an expiation for violating the vow (*avratya*), with the two verses: "Whatever deficiency has occurred in my self... and "Agni has given sight back to me. (30)

Having sprinkled water around the fire from left to right and having placed fuel-sticks of *vaikaṅkata* wood with the *vyāhṛtis*, he satisfies the deities of the *pravargya* with the *madantī* waters. Then, while four fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood—with tips not dried out and smeared with clarified butter—are being placed upon the fire, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite these mantras one by one: "Heaven is the fuel," and so forth. Thereafter, he worships the deities: "O Āditya, lord of vows, I have performed the *śukriya* vow; I was able to do it; may it be successful for me. O Vāyu, lord of vows, I have performed the *śukriya* vow..."

"May that be successful for me! O Agni, Lord of Vows, I have performed the Śukriya vow; may that be successful for me! O Lord of Vows, among all vows, I have performed the Śukriya vow; may that be successful for me! (32)

Having sprinkled water around the fire from left to right and placed fuel-sticks of *vaikaṅkata* wood with the *vyāhṛtis*, and having satiated the deities of the *pravargya* rite with the *madantī* waters, he should perform the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the final *anuvāka*. Then, he should teach him the days on which study is forbidden (*anadhyāya*). He should not study when the sun has set, nor when it has not yet risen, nor when he has traveled abroad, nor when he has returned [from travel], nor in the shadow of clouds, nor in the vicinity of domestic animals, nor of wild animals, nor in the vicinity of water, nor while looking at green barley, nor at mansions, nor at corpses.

Having seen blood produced, he shall not eat meat, nor eat at a funeral feast (*śrāddha*), nor have his hair and beard shaved, nor stretch out his hair, nor brush his teeth, nor apply collyrium, nor anoint himself, nor be wet, nor wear wet clothes, nor [engage in these acts] while wet. 34. Then he should study his sacred recitation (*svādhyāya*): sitting to the west of the fire on *darbha* grass, holding *darbha* grass in his hand, he should study the sacred recitation with his face turned away; having again performed the rite of peace (*śānti*), he should study it. 35.

Now, if he should utter a worldly word, or if at any time he should see someone who has not performed a propitiatory rite (*śānti*), he should perform the *śānti* again and then recite [the Veda]. Having gone out for the *pravargya* with the final [verse], he should not recite anything else until he has re-entered; however, he may recite other [texts] as he pleases. 36. Thus ends the fourth chapter in the third book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the fifth chapter in the third book.
The pacification of the dwelling (*vāstuśamana*) is a repetition of the *prahuta* offering.
(1) When, having stayed for ten nights, he is about to depart—either after ten nights or more—he, together with his wife and his *agnihotra* fires, offers the oblation to Vāstoṣpati and then departs.
(2) Some say that this applies to every one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). (3)
Some say he is a Yāyāvara. 4.
Or, having had a house built, he should first settle in it after pacifying it with the Vāstoṣpatīya rite. 5.

Now some raise the pillars with a sacrificial formula, the rafters with a formula, the roof-coverings with a formula, the wooden beam with a formula, the sleeping-place with a formula, the center of the site with a formula, and the place for the fire with a formula and a non-formula. 6.

If he were to act in this way—just as the Ṛc, Sāman, and Yajus verses, as well as those of the Atharvans and Āṅgirases, are raised up in the assembly and become united as pairs—if he were to settle [the ritual] in that manner, it would be as if he were settling two things that are becoming united as a pair; such would be that which is performed according to the Yajus.
(7) Mental anxieties, physical ailments, seizing spirits, and calamities would strike him down. (8)

Therefore, having caused a silent dwelling to be built, having adorned the doorway, having measured out the center of the site and filled it with earth, and having prepared the place for the couch, he establishes the domestic fire (gṛhyāgni) in the northeast part of the house. Having strewn grass around it and performed the rites up to the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha), he offers oblations from the cooked food. Having recited the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*): "O Lord of the Dwelling (*Vāstoṣpati*), acknowledge us," he offers the oblation with the offering verse (*yājyā*): "O Lord of the Dwelling, with your auspicious assembly... 9. Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*). 10.
O Lord of the Dwelling, you are the firm pillar, the sacrificial session of the Soma-drinkers. The drop is the breaker of eternal fortresses; Indra is the friend of the sages. Svāhā!

11 Whatever fear there is among bipeds, and whatever fear there is among quadrupeds—may Agni, the youngest, drive that fear away. May he grant us well-being for our offspring and well-being for our cattle. Svāhā!

12 Whatever fear there is in the twitching of the eye or the trembling of a limb, whatever fear there is in a curse or in evil speech—may Agni, the youngest, drive that fear away. May he grant us well-being for our offspring and well-being for our cattle. Svāhā! 13

May Agni Yaviṣṭhya drive away that fear which arises from a bad dream, a sinful dream, from the devouring of dreams, and from the sight of impurity. May he grant well-being to our offspring and well-being to our cattle.
Svāhā! O Vāstoṣpati, be our protector; O Indu, increase our household with cattle and horses. May we remain unaging in your friendship. As a father his sons, favor us. Svāhā!
O Vāstoṣpati, bringing us prosperity, entering all forms, be a most gracious friend to us. Svāhā!
The ritual from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards is established as complete up to the granting of the boon by the cow. 17.

Then, in front of the fire, he places the remains of the oblation upon bunches of *darbha* grass with the mantra: "Homage to Rudra, the lord of the dwelling (*vāstoṣpati*), in the coming and the driving away, in the going forth and the departing, in the turning toward and the turning back; I invoke him who protects. 18.

Having poured together the rinsing water from the cooking pot, the remnants of the clarified butter, and the remnants of the water into a vessel, he goes three times around the house clockwise, sprinkling water all around with a branch of the *udumbara* tree, a branch of the *palāśa* tree, a branch of the *śamī* tree, or a handful of *darbha* grass, reciting: "Thou art a sage, thou art a seer; bearing all forms, drive away the fear of men.

(19) Having prepared the food, honored the Brahmins, and caused them to pronounce blessings, [he says]: "May it be auspicious! May it be auspicious! (20) The ritual for the pacification of the site (*vāstuśamana*) has been explained. (21)
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the third book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the sixth chapter in the third book.

Then, having performed the rites from the marking of the place for the sacrifice to the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha), he offers oblations of cooked food with the two verses: "From whatever we fear, O Indra... and "The giver of well-being, the lord of the people... (2).

Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter with the verses: "O Vāstoṣpati...", "O Vāstoṣpati...", "The goddesses...", "Indra and Agni...", "With what splendor will he come to us?", "Who yokes [the horses] today?", and "Be you both of one mind toward us" (3). The rite is completed from the Sviṣṭakṛt offering up to the gift of the cow as a boon (4).
Then, in front of the fire, he places the remnants of the oblation upon *śamī* leaves with the verse, "May the goddesses be for our well-being and aid" (RV 10.9.4).

Having poured together the rinsings of the cooking pot, the remnants of the clarified butter, and the remnants of the water into a vessel, he should pour them out or sprinkle them over those portents with the verse, "We choose that auspiciousness of Śamyoḥ" (RV 10.9.4).
Having prepared food, honored the Brahmins, and caused them to pronounce blessings, he sprinkles [the area] while saying, "Auspicious! Auspicious! (Śivaṃ śivam).
The Adbhuta [rite] has been explained. 8.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the third book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the seventh chapter in the third book.
The *āyuṣyacaru* (oblation for long life) is modeled after the *āhuti* (sacrificial offering). 1.
It should be performed every year, or every six months, or every four seasons, or every month, on the birth-star (*janmanakṣatra*) of the boy. 2.

Then, having performed the rites from the drawing of lines for the sacrificial ground up to the pouring of water for the *praṇītā*, he pours out the rice with the formula: "I pour out what is pleasing to you, Agni Āyuṣmat," or silently. 3.
He pours out the grain with the formula, "I pour you out, acceptable to Prāṇa," or silently.
Having sprinkled them, threshed them, husked them three times, and washed them three times, he sets them aside.
Or he pours out the rice grains.
Having sprinkled them [with water] and washed them three times, he sets them down.
(7) Then, having poured water or milk into the pot across the strainers and placed it over the fire, he pours the rice grains into it across the strainers.
(8) Then he pours out the clarified butter, then places the clarified butter over the fire; having carried fire around both, he cleanses the stirring-spoon and the dipping-spoon. (9)

Then, having cooked this *caru*, having sprinkled it with clarified butter, and having removed it from the fire towards the north, he sprinkles it with clarified butter once it has been set down. This is the procedure for the *caru* for all *sthālīpākas*.

(11) Having performed the rites from the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), he offers from the cooked portion: having recited the invitatory verse (*puro'nuvākyā*), "Bestowing life upon you from every side," he offers with the offering verse (*yājyā*), "O Agni, bestowing life, enjoying the oblation.

(12) Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter; then, having placed the *sthālīpāka* between the fire and the vessel of clarified butter, he pours the residue of the thousand [oblations] over it. (13)

May He who brought forth the Brahman from the Brahman, the Lord of Breath, clad in skin, the wielder of the Pināka bow, the Sovereign God—may He grant us long life; to Him I offer this oblation of clarified butter, Svāhā!

4 He who has come forth, blazing from the midst of the waters, radiant, glowing with the heat of the sun—may that God, casting us away from the terrible noose of Death, protect our life here and consume the clarified butter, Svāhā!

15 The light of Brahman, whom the Lord of Brahman placed as a multiform embryo within the wives of Brahman—the victorious, golden-hued, breaker of darkness, the Sun—we magnify for the sake of long life with clarified butter, Svāhā! 16

We satisfy with clarified butter for the sake of long life here that knowledge which is Śrī, Lakṣmī, Aupalam, Ambikā, Gā, Ṣaṣṭhī, Jayā, and whom they call Indrasenā; she who is of the nature of Brahman and possesses all forms, svāhā!

17 May the daughters of Dakṣa, those of every origin, those of common origin, the thousandfold ones, the multiformed and the uniformed, together with their sons, their lords, and their companions, enjoy this clarified butter here for the sake of long life, svāhā!

18 May the divine hosts, many-formed and ancient, not cut short our lifespan; may they not harm our heroes. To them I offer oblations in many ways with clarified butter; do not harm our progeny nor our heroes, svāhā! 19

That One who was alone in the beginning, from whom the guardians of the world arose—he into whom the world enters at the time of the final transition—may that God consume our oblation of clarified butter here as life; Svāhā!

20 Having offered clarified butter to the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Maruts, Sādhyas, Ṛbhus, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Pitṛs, Viśvedevas, Bhṛgus, Sarpas, and all the Aṅgirases, we have perpetually honored them for the sake of long life; Svāhā!
21 Twenty-six hundred times [repeated], these oblations amount to eight thousand. 22
From the other [portion] that has been cooked, he offers the *sauviṣṭakṛt* oblation.

(23) The rite from the *jaya* offerings onwards is established up to the giving of the cow as a boon. (24) Then, in front of the fire, he places the remnants of the oblation upon clumps of *dūrvā* grass with the two verses beginning, "May [the sacrifice] not harm our great [ones]" and "May [it] not [harm] our offspring. (25)

Sitting to the west of the fire, facing east, with speech restrained and accompanied by his attendants, he eats the *sthālīpāka*. The mantra for its consumption is: "Thou art life; thou art all-life; thou art complete life; thou art total life. May total life be mine; may I attain total life. Having eaten and sipped water, he touches his belly with the two [verses]: "From whatever we fear, O Indra... and "The giver of well-being, the lord of the people... (26).

For the sake of securing well-being for boys seized by malevolent spirits, afflicted by fever, or possessed by ghosts, one should daily recite the *Āyuṣya-ghṛtasūkta* as a study for the purpose of averting calamity; with these very mantras one should offer oblations, and with these very mantras one should present the bali-offerings; thus he indeed becomes free from disease. 27.

This is the *Ṛddha-ayanam* (the path of prosperity) for those possessed by spirits. There are the *Rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings, the *Pañcacoḍa* offerings, the oblation to the serpents (*sarpa*), and the oblation to the Gandharvas. One should recite the daily *Svādhyāya* for the sake of well-being (*svastyayana*). With these very mantras one should offer oblations; with these very mantras one should present the food-offerings (*bali*). Thus, one indeed becomes free from disease. This is the *Ṛddha-ayanam*. Other burnt offerings (*homa*) are imitations of the *Huta* and *Prahuta*; the presentations of food (*baliharaṇa*) are imitations thereof; and the acts of worship (*abhyarcana*) are imitations of the stages of life (*āśrama*), serving as refuges. Thus ends the seventh chapter of the third book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyasūtra*.
Now, in the third book, the eighth chapter:
Now, therefore, on the eighth day of every half-month, Brahmins, celibate students, and women fast for a day. 1.

Then, at dusk, having invoked Rudra Virūpākṣa together with his wife, his sons, his attendants, and his retinue, saying, "I invoke [you]," and having worshipped him with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, he illuminates earthen lamps—one for each person, plus one extra, or four or eight—in every direction within the temple of the god, reciting the two verses beginning with "Shine forth, O Jātavedas; do not harm us," and the two verses beginning with "The bearer of oblations, the subduer of enemies; well-sacrificed, O Agni. (2)

Then, having kindled the fire, he offers of the food that is to be eaten with six verses according to their meters: "These songs for Rudra of the firm bow... (*imā rudrāya sthiradhanvane giraḥ*); with two verses, "Do not [harm] us who are great, nor our offspring" (*mā no mahāntam mā nastoke*); with two verses, "O Lord of the Dwelling, O Lord of the Dwelling" (*vāstoṣpate vāstoṣpate*); and with two verses, "With the moist [weapon], Rudra's missile, Rudra's... (*ārdrayā rudraḥ hetī rudrasya*). These amount to twelve; the year consists of twelve months; verily, he finds support in the year—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"It is known that he places fuel-sticks upon the fire; for trees belong to Viṣṇu, and one attains union with Viṣṇu and residence in his world.
(4) "They praise him with hymns; for the Brahman is indeed the Brahmā-priest, and one attains union with the Brahman and residence in his world.
(5) "He overcomes all evil, he overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin, and he conquers rebirth," so said the venerable Bodhāyana. (6)
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the third book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the ninth chapter in the third book: The Utsarga (concluding rite) is a repetition of the Bali-offering. 1.
It may be performed on the full moon day of Taiṣya or even on that of Māgha.

Having gone out from the village toward the east or the north together with his pupils, and having reached a place where waters flow—having easy landing-stairs, being easy to plunge into, flowing freely, and abounding in shells—he bathes there; sips water; and purifies himself with the *surabhimatī*, the *ābliṅga*, the *vāruṇī*, the *hiraṇyavarṇā*, and the *pāvamānī* verses. Then, having entered into the water, he performs three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) while reciting the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn. Emerging from the water, wringing out his garment, and putting on another clean garment, he sips water again and [offers] water...

Having prepared sacrificial mounds nearby and having handed darbha grass to one another, they prepare seats with darbha grass, saying: "I prepare [a seat] for Brahmā; for Prajāpati; for Bṛhaspati; for Agni; for Vāyu; for Sūrya; for Candramas; for the Nakṣatras; for the Seasons; for the Year; for King Indra; for King Yama; for King Varuṇa; for King Soma; for King Vaiśravaṇa; for the Vasus; for the Rudras; for the Ādityas; for the Viśve Devas; for the Sādhyas; for the Maruts."

"To the Ṛbhus, to the Bhṛgus, to the Atharvans, to the Aṅgirases, to Viśvāmitra, to Jamadagni, to Jāmadagnya, to Bharadvāja, to Gautama, to Ātreya, to Vasiṣṭha, to Kāśyapa, and to Arundhatī, I prepare [this offering]. 3.
Then, to the south: "To Agastya, I prepare [this offering]. 4.

Then, on the north side, wearing the sacred cord over the right shoulder (nivītinaḥ), [he offers] to Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, Jātukarṇya, Tarukṣa, Tṛṇabindu, Somaśuṣmin, Somaśuṣmāyaṇa, Vājin, Vājaśravas, Bṛhaduktha, Varmin, Vajrin, Varūtha, Sanatkumāra, Vāmadeva, Vājiratna, Vīrajit, Haryaśva, Udamegha, Ṛṇañjaya, Tṛṇañjaya, Kṛtañjaya, Dhanañjaya, Satyañjaya, Babhru, Tryaruṇa, Trivarṣa, Tridhātu, and Aśvajña.

To Parāśara, to Mṛtyu, to the Maker, to the Transformer, to the Good Maker, to Tvaṣṭṛ, to Dhātṛ, to Vidhātṛ, to Suśravas, to Sutaśravas, to Satyaśravas, to Savitṛ, to Sāvitrī, to the Metres, to the Ṛgveda, to the Yajurveda, to the Sāmaveda, to the Atharvaveda, to the Atharvāṅgirases, to the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, to the Serpents and the Divine Hosts, and to all beings. 5.

Then, on the south side, with the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he prepares [the offerings] for Vaiśampāyana Phaliṅgu, Tittiri, Ukha, Ukhyāyani, Ātreya the author of the *Padapāṭha*, Kauṇḍinya the author of the *Vṛtti*, Kaṇva, Bodhāyana the author of the *Pravacana*, Āpastamba the author of the *Sūtra*, Satyāṣāḍha, Hiraṇyakeśin, Vājasaneya Yājñavalkya, Bharadvāja, Agniveśya, and the teachers who have drawn up their vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*), for the forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), for those established in their lineage (*vaṃśastha*), and for those whose wives are faithful (*ekapatnī*)—saying, "I prepare [this] for you.
Then, according to their own custom, they prepare [offerings] for their fathers and for their maternal grandfathers.

8. With each of these very names separately, [he worships] with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, saying, "Homage to this one! Homage to that one! 9. [He offers] food, saying, "Svāhā to this one! Svāhā to that one! and fruit-water, saying, "I satiate this one; I satiate that one. 10.
They should recite the first three sections (anuvākas), or all the beginnings of the sections (kāṇḍas).

With the two verses, "Growing up from joint to joint, you spread yourself out by a hundredfold," they plant *dūrvā* grass in the water. Then they wish for one another, saying, "For so-and-so! For so-and-so! (11).
Then, having plunged in, embraced [the water], and made the ocean wavy, they dive three times and run the race to the opposite shore. (12).
Having returned home, they satisfy the Brahmins with cakes, parched grains, flour-meal, and boiled rice, provided that these are available. (13).

They shall not study for three days or one day; they shall not study during the month of Prauṣṭhapada at night, nor constantly during lightning, thunder, and rain—at the occurrence of these three together, or two of them, for three days.
(14) Just as [the suspension] occurs at the commencement (*upākaraṇa*) of the *Chandas* and *Sāman*, so it is at the conclusion (*utsarga*) of the ritual manuals (*kalpa*).
(15) Likewise, at the completion of a *Pārāyaṇa*, except for the planting of *dūrvā* grass at the beginning of the *Kāṇḍa* and the running toward the ocean. (16)
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the third book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the tenth chapter in the third book:
The snake-offering (sarpabali) is indeed a mimicry of the offering of oblations (baliharaṇa). 1.
It should be performed every year, or every six months, or every four seasons, or every month; or it may be performed during the rainy season under the Āśleṣā constellation. 2.
Or the cooking may take place near water or at the top of an anthill. 3.

Having sprinkled [the site] with scented water and water mixed with *dūrvā* grass, and having scattered various *sumanas* flowers, they cook either barley flour, rice flour, or *śyāmāka* millet flour with clarified butter or sugarcane juice to prepare *pāyasa*; then they scatter milk-rice, cakes fried in ghee, boiled rice, parched grains, groats, parched barley-meal, and fried grain-sprouts, reciting the three verses beginning with "Homage be to the serpents" according to their meter.
(4) There are three utterances of "Svāhā": "To the serpents, svāhā! To the *āśreṣās*, svāhā! To the biters, svāhā! (5)

Jīrvara was the *grahapati*, Dhṛtarāṣṭra Hlāvatya the *adhvaryu*, Brahmadatta Tāpasa the *hotṛ*, Pṛthuśravas Dūreśravas the *udgātṛ*, Glāva and Ajaga the *prastotṛ* and *pratihartṛ*, Śitipṛṣṭha the *maitrāvaruṇa*, Takṣaka Vaiśālaki the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*, Upanīti Tārkṣya the *sadasya*, Śikha and Atiśikha the *neṣṭṛ* and *potṛ*, Vāruṇa the *hotṛ-acchāvāka*, Cakra Piśaṅga the *āgnīdhra*, Cāhiro Maheya the *subrahmaṇya*, Arbuda the *grāvastut*, and Sāṇḍa the *unnetṛ*.

With the six formulas, "Paśaga, Dhruvagopa, Kaustuka, Dhurimejaya, Janamejaya—by these very names you are Samīcī, the eastern quarter," and with the six [formulas], "You are the weapons; your houses are in front," and with the formula, "May this oblation be pleasing to the serpents"—thus is the worship performed. (6) Having honored the Brāhmaṇas with threefold food and having caused them to pronounce blessings, (7) the Sarpabali has been explained; the Sarpabali has been explained. (8)
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the third book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the eleventh chapter in the third book:
"Now, these two deities, Prabādhinī and Udvāhikā, are to be worshipped at the time of marriage; for them, that which was prepared for the Sarpabali is provided. (1)

Having fashioned two images of women near water and having adorned them with perfumes and garlands, he worships them in this very manner. (2) The mantra for their worship is: "Those sons, skillful of hand and of noble deeds, brought forth the two great mothers for primordial thought. You two maintain the truth of that which stands and that which moves, according to the law; you protect the station of the son who does not falter. (3) Those wise ones, possessed of creative power and excellent insight, measured out the twin sisters of common origin, the paired ones dwelling in the same abode. As poets of brilliant splendor, they weave a new and ever-new thread within the sky and the ocean. (4)

Then, having taken hold of these [images], having placed them at the side, having carried them forth, and having honored the Brāhmaṇas with threefold food and caused them to pronounce blessings, the sacrifice to the Yakṣīs is explained.
5. Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the third book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the twelfth chapter in the third book.
The monthly rite is an imitation of the *aṣṭakā*; it has been explained previously.

Now, regarding rites for prosperity (*abhyudayika*): the procedure is performed from left to right; the sacred thread is worn over the left shoulder (*yajñopavīta*); the *darbha* grass blades have their tips pointing eastward; an even number of Brahmins are invited; sesame seeds are used in place of [the usual] water; the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) is clotted butter (*pṛṣadājya*).
With a vessel provided with a handle, the taking up of water and the dismissal [of the guests] are performed with the formula: "May the ancestors, whose faces are joyful (*nāndīmukha*), be pleased."

"To the Nāndīmukha ancestors, svāhā"—this is the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa) as an assignment. (4) When the receptacles have been swept clean, upon Darbha grass with tips pointing eastward, there is the pouring of the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) in all cases twice each.

(5) Now, in the rites for a single individual (ekoddiṣṭa), there is no offering into the fire, no announcement, no prior invitation, no portion for the gods, no incense, no lamp, no *svadhā*, no salutation, and no cake here. (6)

Having brought all that has been prepared, having had an even number of Brāhmaṇas wash their hands and feet and sip water, and having seated them on seats provided with *darbha* grass, he should take portions from each item once, sprinkle clarified butter over them, and casting embers mixed with ash toward the south, he should offer oblations into them, saying: "To the deceased, to such-and-such a person, and to Yama, svāhā! Thus it becomes both offered and unoffered. 7.

"May there be satisfaction for such-and-such a one"—with these words, there is the receiving and the dismissal of the water. "May it attend upon such-and-such a one"—this is the assignment. The offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) is indeed upon the [designated] seats. "Be satisfied"—with this, the rinsing takes place. "May there be satisfaction"—this is the dismissal. "May there be satisfaction"—this is the response of the others. (8) From the second day onwards, for the deceased, there is an increase by one each time in the number of Brāhmaṇas fed until the tenth day.
(9) At this point, the new [thread] should be cut off. (10)

On the eleventh day [of the lunar fortnight], the first *śrāddha* is performed; on the third fortnight, the second; and thus, by performing it once every month, they carry it out for eleven months continuously, but they do not extend it into the twelfth month. (11) In the course of a year, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is performed, accompanied by the *agnaukaraṇa*, the *abhiśrāvaṇa*, the *pūrva*, the *daiva*, the incense (*dhūpa*), the lamp (*dīpa*), the *svadhā* invocation, the salutation (*namaskāra*), and the cakes (*apūpa*). (12) Moreover, they cite this: "In the *ekoddiṣṭa* and the *navaśrāddha*, the *agnaukaraṇa* is not desired; one should not perform the *abhiśrāvaṇa*, nor should one cause the *pūrva* to be performed. (13)
One should not perform a prostration, nor likewise utter the *svadhā* formula; after one year has passed, the deceased attains the status of a *pitṛ*.
14. Thus, these analogies have been explained.
15. Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the third book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyasūtra.
Now, the thirteenth chapter in the third book:

Regarding the rites beginning with the ritual cohabitation during the fertile period, or from birth onwards, a boy might have his rites omitted; in such a case, there should be only the initiation (*upanayana*). One should not perform those various individual rites separately, nor should one attempt to accomplish all the rituals in a single oblation. (1) If one were to accomplish all the rituals in a single oblation, one should offer two *mindāhuti* oblations at the beginning of each principal rite. (2)

Having offered the Mindā oblations, the Jayas, and the Abhyātānas; and at the end of the Rudra oblation, it is known: "Rudra is indeed the cruel one among the gods; he becomes pleased and gratified with him. It is known that in all cases involving cutting, splitting, digging, throwing away, or rites for the ancestors, Rākṣasas, Nairṛtas, the Rudras, or malevolent sorcery, one should touch water, for it is stated in the Brāhmaṇa: "Water is indeed peaceful; by means of what is peaceful, he pacifies his impurity.

Up to the sixteenth year for a Brāhmaṇa, up to the twenty-second for a Kṣatriya, and up to the twenty-fourth for a Vaiśya, there is no lapse [of the Sāvitrī]; beyond this, they become those who have fallen from the Sāvitrī (patitasāvitrīkāḥ).
They should not initiate them, they should not teach them, they should not give them their daughters in marriage, and they should not officiate at their sacrifices.
(6) Having caused them to sacrifice with the Trivṛt Vrātyastoma, they should then give them their daughters in marriage.

(7) Whatever rites there may be for those of the same lineage, and for all others, including the propitiatory rites, as well as the auspicious ceremonies such as birth and so forth, these must be performed for the maidens. (8)
"For Brahminhood consists of action; Brahman is said not to be without action, Brahman is said not to be without action.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the third book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyasūtra.

Now, the seasonal coupling and so forth; it is an imitation of the Aṣṭakā rites. Now, these two deities; the Sarpabali is indeed an imitation of the Bali-offerings. The Utsarga is an imitation of the Bali-offerings. Now, therefore, every half-month; the Āyuṣyacaru is an imitation of the Āhuti offerings. Now, if [a plant] should sprout in the house; the Vāstuśamana is an imitation of the Prahuta offerings. Now, therefore, we shall explain the intermediate consecration (avāntaradīkṣā); it lasts for forty-eight days. Impelled by the teacher, he performs the ritual acts. The Upākarma is an imitation of the Huta offerings. 13.

The *upākarma* (commencement of study) is an imitation of the *huta* sacrifice. Impelled by his teacher, he performs the ritual acts; it is measured at forty-eight [days]. Now, therefore, we shall explain the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*). The *vāstuśamana* (pacification of the site) is an imitation of the *prahuta* sacrifice. Now, if a pillar in the house should break, the *āyuṣyacaru* (oblation for long life) is an imitation of the *āhuta* sacrifice. Now, therefore, [this is performed] every half-month. The *utsarga* (concluding rite) is an imitation of the *baliharaṇa* (offering of oblations). The *sarpabali* (serpent offering) is likewise an imitation of the *baliharaṇa*. Now, regarding these deities: the *aṣṭakā* (eighth-day rite) is an imitation [of them]. Now, beginning with the seasonal intercourse [with one's wife], etc. 13. Thus ends the third book of the *Bodhāyana-Gṛhyasūtra*.
Now begins the first chapter of the fourth book.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the expiations for the seven *pākayajñas*.

In that regard, if at the very beginning, after the ground has been smeared, a dog or a cat should pass over it, or if an insect should form a lump [of earth], then having smeared it again, he sprinkles it with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I sprinkle thee with the splendor of Agni. Having thus sprinkled and smeared the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), he should then level the mound.

If the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) has been excavated and a white horse, or some other beast of prey, should scatter [the earth] or step upon it, he sprinkles that footprint with water and mutters: "O Earth, place of sacrifice for the gods! May I not harm the root of your plant.
(3) Then he proceeds according to the established rule.
(4) Now, if the vessel for the *praṇītā* waters should break, he consecrates it with the mantra: "The Gharma is unbroken, the giver of life; from where it was taken, there it has gone back again. (5)
Then, on another occasion, he recites: "May the heat reach the gods," and having filled [the vessel], he worships it with the *vyāhṛtis*.

(6) Now, if the *praṇītā* waters, while being brought forward or once brought forward, should be spilled, he consecrates them with the mantra: "You are imperishable; for the sake of preservation, may you not perish for me in that world, in yonder world.

(7) Having filled [the vessel] again, he worships it with the mantra: "O Earth, sustain my life-span; sustain my breath; sustain my progeny; sustain my cattle. May my life-span, my breaths, my progeny, and my cattle not be spilled away. (8)

Now, if the girl should fall while being seated or while being carried away, they should raise her up with the verse: "The goddess Aditi, of all forms, has risen; she has bestowed long life upon the lord of the sacrifice, preparing a portion for Indra, Mitra, and Varuṇa.

(9) Now, if the girl should become menstruating while being seated or while being carried away, he addresses her with the mantra: "Mitra and Varuṇa are males; both Aśvins are males; Indra and Sūrya are males; may they cause the male [offspring] to prosper. (10)

Now, if the maiden should shed tears while being seated near the fire or while being carried away, he addresses her with this mantra: "The living ones weep; they exert themselves at the sacrifice. The men have fixed their thoughts upon a long-lasting lineage. A blessing to the fathers who have prepared this; a joy for the husbands, as the wives embrace them. (11) Thus ends the first chapter of the fourth book in the Bodhāyana Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the second chapter of the fourth book.

In all cases, if there is burning, damage, loss, or destruction of the ladle, the bunch of grass, the sacrificial strew, the enclosing sticks, the sacrificial grass, the strainers, the fuel, or the ritual materials, one should prepare another according to its characteristic marks and place it down according to its characteristic marks; then one should offer oblations with the wooden spoon using these verses: "O Agni, you [are] ours," "So you [are] ours, O Agni," "O Agni, you are the unswerving one," and "O Prajāpati.
Now, if there is a burning of the sacrificial strew, one should offer an oblation with the words, "To Agni Kṣāmavat, svāhā! and then strew the grass around the fire.
Having strewn the grass around the fire with the two verses, "Indra for you from every side" and "Indra, the men," one offers an oblation with the words, "To Indra, svāhā!"

Now, if the enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) is burnt, he offers another one, having placed it according to its characteristic mark, with the verse: "O Agni, having surrounded us with thy fortress... (RV 10.87.22).

Now, if there is damage by fire, loss, or destruction of the sprinkled garments, he prepares another garment according to its characteristic mark, places it according to its characteristic mark, and offers it with the formula: "To the thread, svāhā! (TS 3.1.4.3). If there should be a blow from a *sic* (a fringe or border), he consecrates it with the mantra: "Thou art a *sic*, thou art a thunderbolt in the nose; homage be to thee, do not harm me. Having taken up the thread of the fringe, he should blow upon it with his mouth. (TS 3.1.4.4–5)

Now, if a cow, or a horse, or a dog, deer, buffalo, ram, boar, or any other tusked beast of prey should pass by keeping him to his left, he sprinkles its footprint with water and mutters: "That is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu" (Tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam).

Or he may utter a verse addressed to Rudra; he should either offer oblations or mutter two verses addressed to Rudra: "Thou, O Agni, art Rudra" (Tvaṃ agne rudraḥ) and "Protect the King" (Ā vo rājānam).

Now, if a bird should utter a cry, he addresses that speech with the mantra: "May our bipeds and quadrupeds all be free from disease; like a singer of the Sāman, O bird, you sing; like a son of the Brahman, you recite at the libations. May it be well for us, O bird; be well-disposed toward us. (9) Then, if a female jackal should howl, he addresses her with the mantra: "Long-snouted one, evil-jawed one, do not speak from the south! If you speak from the south, may you drive away my enemy. (10)

Now, if he should be desirous [of averting evil], then upon sneezing or coughing, having touched water, he should mutter: "The call after, the call around, the reproach, the destruction, the bad dream, the ill-spoken word—this I direct against my enemies. The call following, the call around, O bird, whatever was inauspicious, the sidelong course of the deer—this I direct against my enemies. (11)

Then, when crossing rivers and deserts, he mutters the prayer for protection from the front: "The herbs that there are, the trees that there are, the rivers that there are, the deserts that there are, and the forests—that [all these], O bride, may release you, rich in offspring, from distress.

(12) Then, when crossing dung, he mutters the prayer for protection from the front: "Homage to Rudra who dwells in dung; homage to him who dwells in dung! You deserve a cow; let there be homage to you; do not harm me! (13)

Now, when passing by a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), a standing pillar (*sthāṇu*), or a crossroads (*catuṣpatha*), he mutters the following prayer of approach: "The sacred bathing place has been made, with good drinking water, O Lords of Beauty! May it strike down the pillar on the path and evil intent.

(14) Now, when passing by various auspicious marks (*lakṣaṇa*), he mutters the following prayer of approach: "Those gods and goddesses who dwell in these trees—may they bring me prosperity and increase of fortune; may they not harm me, carrying me forward while being mindful of me. (15) Then he proceeds directly to the conclusion of the ritual act. (16)
Thus ends the second chapter in the fourth book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the third chapter in the fourth book:
In all cases, when the fire has been kindled by itself, he places two fuel-sticks upon it with the two verses beginning, "Shine forth, O Jātavedas. 1.

Then, having passed beyond the cremation ground and other such places, he kindles that very same fire, strews grass around it, and having performed the rites up to the *agnimukha*, he offers oblations from the cooked food with the formulas: "Agni, lord of beings, may he protect me, svāhā! Indra, lord of the eldest, may he protect me, svāhā!

(2) The rite is completed from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering down to the gift of the cow as a boon. (3) Then he addresses this couple with the mantra: "May this couple be long-lived; may this couple be possessed of offspring; may this couple be possessed of cattle; may this couple be possessed of vigor. (4)
Then, with the verse, "Upward that Jātavedas," he yokes the ox on the right; having yoked the left one with the verse, "The bright face of the gods has risen," he sets out.

(5) Now, if there is a crossing by boat at a ford, he consecrates it with the mantra: "May this Lord of the Forest lead us safely to the further shore of the great river; become easy for us to cross, for long life and for splendor. He gazes upon the bride as she crosses by boat. (6) Having crossed to the bank, he mutters: "Homage to the ocean, the guide, the lord of rivers! (7)
Having set out upon a difficult road, he worships the sun with the verse "To Jātavedas" (RV 1.50.1) one thousand times.

||8|| When danger is imminent, during a deceptive game of dice, in the royal court, in times of misfortune, or when bound, he should mutter this very same [verse] continuously and in a low voice. In the case of bad dreams, he should mutter this very same [verse] one hundred times.
||9|| Thus ends the third chapter in the fourth book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the fourth chapter of the fourth book of questions.

Now, if there should be an attack or if the fire should go out, having sprinkled [the site] with the words, "All that has been struck down," and having leveled the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), he kindles that very same fire, strews grass around it, and having performed the rites up to the *agnimukha*, he offers oblations from the cooked food with the three verses beginning, "Those gods who strike the sacrifice, who steal the sacrifice," according to their respective meters.
From the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the procedure is established until the giving of the cow as a boon.

Now, if there should be a breakage of the dice, one should kindle that very same fire, strew grass around it, and having performed the preliminary offerings beginning with the mouth of the fire, he offers the principal oblations with the formulas: "Here is support, svāhā! Here is separation, svāhā! Here is delight, svāhā! Here is rejoicing, svāhā! (3).
The rite is completed from the *jaya* offering up to the gift of the cow and the granting of the boon.
(4) Then he brings another die with the formula: "You are undecaying; for the sake of non-decay, may you not be exhausted for me in yonder world, in that world. (5)
Then he yokes him to the chariot with the verse: "Mount the chariot, O slayer of Vṛtra! (RV 10.103.1).

Then he establishes a couple upon the chariot with the formula: "I establish myself in sovereign power, I establish myself in the kingdom; I establish myself in the horses, I establish myself in the cattle; I establish myself in the limbs, I establish myself in the self; I establish myself in offspring, I establish myself in what is to be.
As before, he yokes the two oxen. Having thus established the couple, he sets forth.

Now, if he is able to contend with one who is stronger, he causes the chariot to move forward along the path, [reciting]: "May we be debtless in this world, debtless in the next, and debtless in the third world. May we pass through all paths—those that go to the gods and those that go to the fathers—being debtless. (9) Then, having halted on the path, he mutters for the sake of setting out: "We have entered upon the path of the pair that brings well-being, the path that leads to well-being and is free from danger, by which one avoids all enemies and finds wealth. (10) Then he approaches the chariot, [reciting]: "The protector of every path... (11)

Now, if there should be terror at the flash of lightning and the thunder, he mutters the two Aindrī verses from the *Tamas* section: "From whatever we fear, O Indra... and "The giver of well-being, the lord of the people... (RV 7.87.1; 6.47.11). Then he proceeds with the conclusion of the ritual.
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the fourth book in the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyasūtra*.

Now begins the fifth chapter of the fourth book: the expiation for domestic sacrifices (*pākayajña*). 1. Regarding this, one should offer oblations with the following mantras—*ātmano jyotiḥ*, *ayāścāgne*, *yadasminkarmaṇi*, *svasti na indro vṛddhaśravāḥ*, and the *vyāhṛtis*—in the event that the sacrificial materials, the oblation, the mantras, the ritual acts, and so forth, have been omitted, spilled, broken, shattered, lost, spoiled, inverted, burnt, not properly cooked, or improperly cut; and in the case of rites for which no specific rule has been prescribed. 2. One should offer with these mantras: *ātmano jyotiḥ*, *ayāścāgne*, *yadasminkarmaṇi*, *svasti na indro vṛddhaśravāḥ*, and the *vyāhṛtis*.

The teachers declare that when the *vyāhṛtis* are employed, it becomes exactly as it was performed. 3. Regarding this, they cite examples: *bhūḥ* for the *ṛc*s, *bhuvaḥ* for the *yajus*s, and *suvaḥ* for the *sāman*s. 4.
Bodhāyana says that one should offer [the oblation] at the beginning of the principal part once the ritual action has commenced. 5.
"Up to the end of the *pradhāna* offerings," says Śālīki.
"Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering," says Aupamanyava.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the fourth book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the sixth chapter of the fourth book.

Now, regarding the rites of conception (*garbhādhāna*), the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the offering to Viṣṇu (*viṣṇubali*), the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), the naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first outing (*upaniṣkramaṇa*), the first feeding (*annaprāśana*), the tonsure (*coḍa*), the initiation (*upanayana*), and so forth—if one does not have these performed, the procedure is the same: then one should offer as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) the *āpaḥ*, the *yatpākatrā*, the *manasvatī*, two *mindāhuti* oblations, the *mahāvyāhṛtis*, and the *vyāhṛtis*.
(1) In the event of a lapse of time, one should offer two *mindāhuti* oblations each at the beginning of the principal rites. (2)

"And preceded by the *vyāhṛtis*—this is common to all," so the teachers declare. Regarding this, they cite as examples: "The cooked *sauviṣṭakṛta* offering, the carrying forward of the *praṇītā* water, the *brāhmaṇa*, the fuel and sacrificial grass (*idhmā-barhis*), and the single [offering]"—thus it is known; for so says the *Brāhmaṇa*, for so says the *Brāhmaṇa*. Thus ends the sixth chapter in the fourth book of the *Bodhāyana Gṛhyasūtra*.
Now begins the seventh chapter of the fourth book.

Now, regarding the reversal of the spreading of *darbha* grass, the making of the *pavitra*, the placing of the vessels, the consecration of the *prokṣaṇī* water, the *brahman* and the *praṇītā* waters, the pouring out of the sacrificial food (*havis*), the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*), the wiping of the *sruk* ladles, the sprinkling around with the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), and the placing of the fuel-wood (*idhma*)—if these are performed in reverse, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is as follows: one should offer the "Tataṃ me" verse, the "Āpaḥ," the "Yatpākatrā," the "Manasvatī," the two *mindāhuti* oblations, the *mahāvyāhṛtis*, and the *vyāhṛtis* as expiation; thus says Baudhāyana.
(1) Thus ends the seventh chapter of the fourth book in the Baudhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra.
Now begins the eighth chapter of the fourth book.

Now we shall explain the expiations (*prāyaścitta*). If a broken, lost, defective, inverted, or cracked sacrificial post; or a dog, cat, crow, donkey, wild animal, domestic animal, bird, reptile, or any other insect should pass between the officiating priests and the fires, one should offer oblations with the *Durgā*, the *Manasvatī*, the three *Mahāvyāhṛtis*, and the *Tantumatī* verses. That indeed is the expiation for that. 1.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the fourth book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the ninth chapter of the fourth book:
Hereafter, we shall explain the collection of expiations for the seven pākayajñas. 1.

The *huta*, *prahuta*, *āhuta*, *śūlagava*, *baliharaṇa*, *pratyavarohaṇa*, and the *aṣṭakā-homa*—these are the seven *pākayajñas*. In these, neither the *prayājas* nor the *anuyājas* are offered, nor are there *sāmidhenī* verses.
(2) When the ritual acts have been commenced, having kindled the fire and strewn grass around it, wherever one performs a *darvī-homa*, one takes a portion from the *caru* and offers it.

(3) In all cases, if there is a spill, a breakage, a cutting, a scorching, a transposition, a burning out, a deficiency or excess, or the loss of the *pavitra* strainer, or the breaking of a vessel, one offers two *mindā-hutis*. (4)
If [the clarified butter] should be spoiled by flies, mosquitoes, hairs, or ants, one should perform an oblation to Prajāpati.
(5) If the clarified butter has been spoiled, or if it has become contaminated and its atonement is unknown, one performs the *yajñasamṛddhī* oblations.
(6) In the event of an interruption, one performs the atonement by offering the *daśahotṛ* and the *anukhyā*. (7)
If [the fire] has gone out, he performs the expiation by offering the *caturhotṛ* and the *anukhyā*.
(8) If a frog, a snake, a mouse, or a cat passes between [the fires], he performs the expiation by offering the *pañcahotṛ* and the *anukhyā*.
(9) If there is a deformed appearance, a deformed sound, or a crackling noise, he performs the expiation by offering the *śaṃyuvāka* and the *anukhyā*. (10)

The universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) for an unordained act has been explained; one should designate it as "Vāruṇī. (11) At the end of the consecrations, if the fire has gone out, one should deposit its ashes [into a new fire], or if one cannot find a sacrificial fuel-stick (*samidh*), one performs the sacrificial expiation consisting of the Mahāvyāhṛtis, the *praṇava*, and the Manasvatī verse. (12) In the event of errors regarding tone, syllables, words, or meters, [one offers] with the verse beginning "With these songs" (*ābhir gīrbhiḥ*). (13)
In all *pākayajña* sacrifices, one should give a cow, a bull, or an ox to the members of the assembly (*sadasya*).
(14) This is because the members of the assembly will instruct [the sacrificer] regarding all expiations and substitutes.
(15) Thus ends the ninth chapter in the fourth book of the *Bodhāyana Gṛhyasūtra*.
Now, the tenth chapter of the fourth book:

Now, if at the times of the oblations the fire should go out, one should sprinkle everything with water, saying, "May [the fires] drive away that," then clear the sacrificial mound, establish the fire, and having strewn grass around it, one performs the expiation. One should offer the expiation consisting of the *ayāsya* verse, the five *hotṛ*-formulas, the *brāhmaṇa ekahotā*, the ten *manasvatī* verses, the two *mindāhuti* offerings, the *mahāvyāhṛtis*, and the *vyāhṛtis*. Thus one should perform the expiation. 1.

Now, if the fire of initiation (*upanayana*), the marriage fire (*vivāha*), the birth fire (*jātakāgni*), or the cremation fire (*śmaśānāgni*) should go out before the fourth day, the tenth day, or until the piling of the funeral mound (*sañcayana*), one should sprinkle it with water while reciting, "Struck down are the Asuras," and quickly consign it to the ashes. Having consigned it to a fuel-stick (*samit*) with the verse, "This is thy seasonal womb," and having brought a common worldly fire (*laukika-agni*), one places a fuel-stick upon it with the two verses, "Being invoked" (*ājuhvānaḥ*) and "Awake, O Agni" (*udbudhyasva*). 2.

Having strewn [the sacrificial grass] all around, he offers the expiation-oblations: *ayāścāgne*, the Pañcahotṛ-formula, the Brāhmaṇa-ekahotṛ-formula, the ten Manasvatī-formulas, two Mindā offerings, the Mahāvyāhṛtis, and the Vyāhṛtis; "one should offer the expiation-oblations," says Baudhāyana.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the fourth book of the Baudhāyana Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the eleventh chapter in the fourth book.

Now, for a householder or a student, when the fire has gone out, when the time for the two offerings of the New and Full Moon sacrifices has passed, when one has not yet performed the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, when there is the consumption of new grain, when clarified butter has been spilled, when a ritual act has been omitted, when a mantra has been dropped, when an act has been performed redundantly, when a wife has given birth before the *Sīmanta* ceremony was performed, when twins are born among women or cattle, when one has had intercourse with a woman during her menstrual period, when one has conversed with an outcast, when one has had sexual intercourse by day, when one has had intercourse with a *Śūdra* woman, when semen is emitted at the end of a dream, when one urinates or defecates in water, or in the case of a young boy—

For one who has been born [into the order] but fails to perform the purificatory rites (*asaṃskāra*), for failing to establish contact with the sacred fires (*akṛtāgnisaṃsarga*), for an inversion of deities (*devatāviparyāsa*), an inversion of mantras (*mantraviparyāsa*), or an inversion of ritual acts (*karmaviparyāsa*); for a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) who fails in his vows (*vrataviparyāsa*), for the breaking of the girdle or the sacrificial cord (*mekhalāyajñopavīta*), for the failure to wear the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), for the failure to carry the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), for the breaking of the staff (*daṇḍabhaṅga*), for the omission of the twilight prayers (*sandhyālopa*), for the omission of the fire-ritual (*agnikāryalopa*), for the omission of the water-jar (*udakumbhalopa*), for the omission of begging for alms or the private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāyalopa*), for the omission of service (*śuśrūṣālopa*), and for these and other such unrecorded transgressions, there is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). 1.

Having kindled the fire and strewn it around, he offers the expiation oblations: "Protect us from sin, O Agni, svāhā! Protect us, O All-Knowing One, svāhā! Protect the sacrifice, O Radiant One, svāhā! Protect everything, O Lord of a Hundred Powers, svāhā! Protect us with one [flame], O Agni; protect us also with a second; protect us with three songs, O Lord of Strength; protect us with four, O Vasu, svāhā! (2) Both before and after, including the preliminary sequence, so that the performance proceeds in due order, uninterrupted and continuous. (3)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the fourth book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the twelfth chapter of the fourth book:
Now we shall explain the expiation for the interruption of the ritual intercourse during the fertile period (*ṛtu*) of a householder who is a student and has been authorized by his wife. 1.

Having announced the seasonal periods—spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn, winter, and the cool season—to the Brahmins, and having completed the observance of his vows, he then leads them at nightfall to the place of sacrifice. 2.

Then, having performed the rites from the marking out of the sacrificial ground up to the "mouth of the fire" (the *āghāra* libations), he offers an oblation of cooked food, reciting as the invitatory verse (*puro'nuvākyā*) "He who, honoring thee with a yearning heart... and offering with the offering verse (*yājyā*) "To whomsoever thou, O Jātavedas, for the sake of the well-doer...
3. Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter, beginning with "Madhu and Svāhā! Mādhava and Svāhā! and continuing to the end of the section. 4.
The rite from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards is established up to the giving of the cow as a gift.
(5) To the west of the fire, both the husband and wife should consume the remainder of the clarified butter and the remainder of the water.
(6) The expiation for the interruption of the ritual union during the fertile period has been explained. (7)

Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the fourth book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyasūtra. Now, concerning the householder; now, concerning the master of the household; now, if [the rites are performed] at the times for the burnt offerings (homa); now, therefore, regarding the seven pākayajñas; now, the expiations (prāyaścitta); now, the irregularities; now, the impregnation rite (garbhādhāna); now, regarding the pākayajñas; now, the accidental interruption; everywhere [the sacrificer acts] himself; everywhere [the offering is made with] a ladle; now, therefore, regarding the seven pākayajñas. 12.

Now, therefore, [the section] on the seven *pākayajñas*. In all cases, the sacrificial ladle (*darvī*). In all cases, [the sacrificer] himself. Now, the supplementary oblation (*abhyāghāta*). Now, regarding the *pākayajñas*. Now, the *garbhādhāna* (conception rite). Now, the *viparīta* (rite for reversing misfortune). Now, the expiations (*prāyaścittas*). Now, therefore, [the section] on the seven *pākayajñas*. Now, if at the times of the *homa*s... Now, the householder (*gṛhamedhin*). Now, the duties of the householder. 12. Thus ends the fourth book (*praśna*) in the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyasūtra*;
thus the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyasūtra* is completed.
